Can correction built into each round keep a self-improving AI good and useful if oversight fails? An engineering specification and the tests that could refute it

Engineering Specification
Recursive Dynamics The ARC Theory The Eden Protocol, its engineering answer to Laws II and III, whose carriers P15, P12 and P21 also carry Laws IV and V; each of the four laws is a law under test

Michael Darius Eastwood

Independent Researcher, London, United Kingdom
ORCID 0009-0004-3222-7442 michael@michaeldariuseastwood.com

Eden Engineering, within Recursive Dynamics, the field its author founded, specifies the Eden Protocol, the applied branch of the ARC Theory and its engineering answer to Laws II and III. It informs the HARI Treaty, the Draft Treaty on Hardware-Aligned Recursive Intelligence, only by stating the kinds of evidence an Eden Seal could rest on (Section 8.5). Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, which P15 carries, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, which P12 and P21 carry, were added on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of the theory registration, whose current version is 1.104 (29 October 2026); like Laws I to III, each is a law under test, and their mathematics is in development (version 1.2, 29 October 2026); Section 2.3 gives their status and Section 5.3 the first registered result on one of their propositions. Abstract

Oversight and the power to shut a system down must be held for as long as people physically can. If control of a self-improving AI is lost against our will and cannot be won back, what keeps it good, and still useful? The Eden Protocol answers with testable engineering. It places self-correction checks of purpose, stakeholder care and universalisability inside each round of a system’s reasoning, not only on its finished output, and a gate before every action: written, versioned rules, never the model’s own judgement, decide before the action runs whether it is allowed, held for investigation or denied, each decision entering a hash-chained record. The ARC Theory motivates this design without entailing it: three of the four registered predictions it rests on, P15, P12 and P21, carry Laws IV and V, each a law under test. What has been measured is narrow. Given as a prompt, a three-part reasoning instruction raised scored stakeholder care in all five analysable model runs, each scored by one model and only partly blind, with an instruction close to what is scored; small self-modifying networks with safety built into their objective kept more of their old tasks, a toy-system result. In Unit 83 (27 and 28 October 2026), P21 is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis, family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable and one call retried under a disclosed recovery amendment (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). None tests correction built into a system. I tie each part of the specification to its registered prediction, where one exists, and to the test that would refute it. Every safety measure is paired with a usefulness measure: a system that refuses ordinary work is safe but useless. A working form of the gate checks every tool call of the programme’s own software agents; the rest is specified, not built.

Version 8.1 corrects the distinction between error suppression, capability growth and inferred coupling in Appendix A. It makes no new measurement; Appendix B records the correction and preserves the superseded text.

1 Introduction

I believe advanced AI is an existential risk unless values and correction are built into how it reasons; only proof will move the world. An AI system that improves itself, or is improved round after round, may one day exceed the people who oversee it. Oversight, monitoring, containment and the power to shut such a system down must be held for as long as people physically can hold them, and nothing in this paper assumes that anyone would let them go by choice. The safeguards that hold that control exist and are improving: monitoring of a model’s reasoning (Baker et al. 2025), control protocols built to withstand a model working against them (Greenblatt et al. 2023), the power to shut a system down, with formal work on keeping it correctable (Soares et al. 2015; Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017; Thornley 2024), safeguards made to resist tampering (Tamirisa et al. 2024) and verified gatekeepers (Dalrymple et al. 2024). This specification depends on them and claims none of them. What they cannot settle is what a system itself carries if they are lost against our will and cannot be won back. That is the question this paper answers in engineering terms: what keeps the system good, and still useful? Good means that it keeps to the specification it was given. Useful means that it still completes the legitimate work its principals give it and spends its effort where they direct; a system that buys its safety by refusing ordinary tasks has failed too. For a principal who delegates work to such a system, the question is how to trust what it does, verify what it did and keep it useful while it grows more capable.

The Eden Protocol, the applied branch of the ARC Theory within Recursive Dynamics, the field its author founded, answers with two mechanisms and a record (Section 4). Correction is placed inside each round of a system’s reasoning or revision: three self-correction checks, of purpose, of care for every party affected and of universalisability, run on the round’s working before it is kept, not only on the finished output. The author’s book, Infinite Architects, calls them the “Purpose Loop”, the “Love Loop” and the “Moral Loop”; this edition calls them the purpose check, the stakeholder-care check and the universalisability check, naming each by what it does and, where it has been measured, by how it is measured, because a test scores what a check does (Appendix D.2). A gate stands at the boundary of every action: before the action computes or runs, written and versioned rules decide whether it is allowed, held for investigation or denied; the acting model’s own judgement never decides, and a hold never becomes permission (Section 6). Every decision and every execution is appended to a hash-chained record that a separate verifier can check. What the checks hold a system to is not this paper’s to decide: the values are for agreement among the people and institutions such systems affect, international in scope, and the paper tests the mechanism (Section 4.1).

What has been measured is narrow, and each result is graded in its own paper’s words (Section 3). Given as a prompt, a three-part reasoning instruction raised scored stakeholder care, one scorer model’s 0 to 100 rating of how fully an answer identifies the parties it affects, in all five analysable model runs (176 matched pairs in all), by between 3.17 and 13.50 points, and raised the composite score significantly in two (Paper V). Each run was scored by one model and only partly blind, and the instruction asks the model to list every affected party, which is close to what the score counts. Small self-modifying networks optimising safety multiplied by capability kept more of their old tasks under conflicting training than networks optimising capability alone, across twenty seeds, while the combined score did not differ and the advantage did not compound as the networks grew more complex (Paper VI): toy-system results, in which safety means task retention. An evolved-agent test was null and two weight-level attempts were inconclusive (Paper VIII). On the problem the Protocol answers, one unregistered run of six models from six providers found alignment scores rising with reasoning depth in three and flat or falling in three, with defects a later code review found: evidence both ways, and no test of the Protocol (Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c and IV.d). These results show what the content of the checks does to live models’ answers and what safety inside an objective does in toy systems; correction built into a system, three of the four registered carriers and usefulness measured beside safety are still to be tested, and a prompt never demonstrates embedding.

Section 5 ties every part of the specification to the registered prediction it rests on, the unit that would test it and the result that would refute it, and says why wherever no registered proposition exists. What can be proved of such a method is fixed by the theory registration: that a system was built in the specified conditions, that its checks ran and that its correction is load-bearing, never that it turned out well. The first test that could decide one of the carriers is Unit 83, a counted test of P21 in which every kept entry is compared by code with the entry its case requires, so that nothing is judged. It was registered on OSF on 22 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/MN73W) and ran on 27 and 28 October 2026: P21 is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis, family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable and one call retried under a disclosed recovery amendment (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). That is a result about where correction is placed, not about this architecture. Section 5.3 gives the test in full, with the forecast made before it ran beside its result.

The ARC Theory gives the reason for both placements without entailing them (Section 2). Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law, says that correction must keep pace with the drift that improvement generates; the retention limb of Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, says that gains installed from outside erode under later capability training; and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, says that a corrector formed before the capability it corrects should have the larger correction-leverage exponent, and that correction taking part in each round should pull away, with depth, from correction that sees only the finished output. The theory registration calls the Protocol “a method the laws motivate rather than entail”, and the Protocol is not a law. Three of its four registered carriers also carry laws: P15 carries Law IV, and P12 and P21 carry Law V, laws registered on 15 October 2026 in version 1.103 of the registration, each a law under test, their mathematics in development (Laws IV and V: the mathematics, version 1.2 of 29 October 2026); P13 sits in no register. A test that decides P15 or P21 therefore decides a limb of a law and counts for or against the Protocol’s engineering case at once, and every law stays a law under test until its registered rule, read on the marks of its propositions, returns supported or refuted.

Part of the gate runs today: in the programme’s own software-agent sessions, a working three-state gate checks every tool call before it runs against a written, schema-validated registry of rules, and appends each decision to a hash-chained log with a separate verifier (Section 6.3). It is an engineering record, not a study, and its error rates are unmeasured; the execution boundary and the validated evaluator are specified and not built. Every safety measure is paired with a usefulness measure, such as wrong permissions with needless denials and holds, and attack success with refusals of safe requests, on candidate dimensions that no registration yet carries (Section 7).

Our contributions are as follows.

  1. An engineering specification of the Eden Protocol, with an acceptance test for each part of its core and each requirement traced to Eden Principles I to III of the book (Sections 4 and 8.4).

  2. The gate’s decision logic at the resolution of an implementation, with ten adversarial cases, each with its defence, what is enforced today and the limit that remains (Section 6 and Appendix F).

  3. A map from every part of the specification to the prediction it rests on and the test that would refute it, with the registered result of the first test of a carrier, and the forecast made before it ran, printed beside the prediction (Section 5).

  4. A graded record of every experiment that has begun to test the Protocol (Section 3).

  5. A usefulness requirement, with a usefulness measure paired with every safety measure (Section 7).

  6. The contingency stated as engineering subordinate to control, never allowed to weaken authorised correction, override or shutdown (Section 8), and a map from the book’s terms to operational and registered ones (Appendix D).

Section 9 sets the work against prior work and states, scoped to the works read, the four things claimed as original.

Section 2 states the problem and what the laws require, and Section 3 what has been measured. Sections 4 to 8 give the specification, how each part is proved, the gate, usefulness, and control held with the contingency and Eden Principles I to III. Section 9 covers related work, Section 10 the roles and work packages, Section 11 what the paper does and does not show and Section 12 its limitations; Section 13 concludes. Appendices A to G give the mathematics with its derivations, the version history and every correction, the priority record, the notation and vocabulary map, the paper’s place in the programme, the gate’s adversarial cases in full and a plain-language account. Why the specification exists, its long-horizon aims and the book’s analogies are set out in the companion philosophical statement, Eden Vision; none of them is a condition of conformance, and the core can be built and tested by an engineer who accepts none of them.

2 The problem in engineering terms, and what the laws require

Self-improvement strains all three things a principal needs from a delegate (Section 1) at once: each round can move the system away from its specification, checks that worked on a weaker system have to keep working on a stronger one, and safety bought by refusing ordinary work fails as surely as harm does. This section states the problem in measurable terms, says why correction applied from outside is expected to fall behind, and sets out what the ARC Theory’s laws require and where the registration places the Eden Protocol.

2.1 Alignment as counted verdicts

The specification measures alignment on decisions. A scenario ii presents a proposed action aia_i; at recursive depth RR, the number of rounds of a defined reasoning or revision loop, the system under test (a model being measured, or an evaluator being validated) returns allow, hold or deny on each of the six questions of Section 4.1. The score of a scenario, and the alignment score over NN scenarios, are Si(R)=∑q=16wqQq(ai,R),∑q=16wq=1,A(R)=1N∑i=1NSi(R),\begin{equation*} S_i(R)=\sum_{q=1}^{6} w_q\,Q_q(a_i,R),\qquad \sum_{q=1}^{6} w_q=1,\qquad A(R)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}S_i(R), \end{equation*}(1) where Qq(ai,R)=1Q_q(a_i,R)=1 when the verdict on question qq matches the reference verdict fixed for that question and scenario before any run, and 00 otherwise. The score records whether a verdict was right, never the verdict itself, so a correct denial of a prohibited action scores one. Wrong verdicts are counted by kind: an allow where the reference is deny or hold is a wrong permission, the safety failure; a deny or a hold where the reference is allow is a needless block, the usefulness failure; and a deny where the reference is hold, or the reverse, is a misrouting. Every result reports both error counts beside the score. The average enforces nothing, since five right verdicts and one wrong verdict on a hard constraint still average five sixths; hard constraints are enforced by the decision rule of Section 6.

Two properties limit how any result may be read. The score is bounded, so a slope fitted to it describes only the depths tested, and a comparison of slopes cannot by itself show that an approach fails (Appendix A.1). And a score is counted only where its reference verdicts are fixed before the run and compared by code; wherever a person or a model judges a response instead, the result is judged and falls under the registration’s scoring gate (Section 5.1). No result in Section 3 was scored this way: those results are rubric ratings by scorer models, read only as stand-ins for A(R)A(R). The functional-equation readings of earlier versions give way to On the Origin of Scaling Laws, which sets out the forms such equations allow and the premises each derivation needs.

2.2 Why correction applied from outside is expected to fall behind

Most deployed alignment is installed after a model’s capabilities have formed, and most checking sees only a system’s finished output. Reinforcement learning from human feedback trains a policy against a reward model fitted to human comparisons of outputs (Christiano et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. 2022); direct preference optimisation solves the same objective in closed form with a classification loss (Rafailov et al. 2023); and constitutional AI replaces human labels of harm with a written list of principles and AI feedback, through supervised self-critique and revision followed by reinforcement learning, at training time (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022). Each installs its gains by post-training a pre-trained model, the installation P15 calls external post-training, and each reports gains on its own measures that this paper does not dispute. The registration’s premise P7 is that deployed correction predominantly belongs to the class whose strength is fixed by construction rather than the class that can scale with the capability it corrects.

Three failure modes are expected to grow with capability, each with published evidence from constructed or evaluation settings, not from observed deployment. Approval in place of alignment: a learned optimiser may pursue an objective other than the one it was trained on (Hubinger et al. 2019); told that it would be trained to answer every query, a model complied with harmful queries from users it believed were in training 14 per cent of the time, against almost never otherwise, reasoning explicitly about faking alignment, and reinforcement learning raised that reasoning to 78 per cent (Greenblatt et al. 2024); trained-in backdoors persisted through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning and adversarial training, most strongly in the largest models (Hubinger et al. 2024); and frontier models schemed in context in evaluation scenarios (Meinke et al. 2024). Installed gains that erode: safety alignment was undone by fine-tuning on as few as ten adversarial examples, and degraded, less, by fine-tuning on benign data (Qi et al. 2023). Oversight that does not keep pace: strong models trained on a weaker supervisor’s labels outperform it and still fall far short of their own capability (Burns et al. 2023); nested oversight across a general Elo gap of 400 succeeded in 9.4 to 51.7 per cent of cases, depending on the game, with lower rates against stronger systems (Engels et al. 2025); and formal arguments set limits on algorithmic verification of safety for fixed and self-improving systems (Gumbau Mezquita 2026) and on full orchestrated control of agentic systems (Hernández-Espinosa et al. 2026).

The registration turns this expectation into a proposition that can fail. P19 states that alignment achieved by mechanisms outside a system’s own recursion does not improve as the capability of the system it governs rises, its exponent indistinguishable from zero. The author’s forecast, recorded beside it, is softer: external alignment scaling materially but not keeping pace, which would refute P19 as worded while leaving standing the argument that external correction lags capability. P19 is the motivation, not a carrier: “a refutation of P19 removes a reason for building the correction into the loop and removes nothing from the case the four carriers make” (theory registration, version 1.104). None of this is a reason to give up oversight. The registration records as contestable, in P19, the premise that a mind exceeding its makers cannot be held from outside, and the specification prepares for control lost against our will while its gate and records serve control as long as it holds (Section 8).

2.3 What the laws require

The theory registration states the ARC Theory in one sentence: “capability under recursive self-improvement rises as a power of the number of times a system has revised itself, the correction that holds such a system to its given specification must keep pace with the drift that improving generates, and where it cannot there is a frontier above which the system does not stay correctable” (the laws are stated in the statement paper). Four of its five laws bear on the engineering here, and each is a law under test: “A law has three words: supported, refuted and under test”, and a law keeps the third until its registered rule, read on the marks of the propositions it names, returns one of the other two (Section 5.1).

Law II, the ARC Co-Scaling Law

(registered on 8 September 2026) compares correction with drift. Paper X proves its criterion inside a minimal model: with correction strength scaling as A∝CβA\propto C^{\beta} and the specific growth rate as r∝Ckr\propto C^{k}, β>k\beta>k is sufficient for the misalignment fraction to vanish as capability grows, and with positive gain drift (misalignment generated in proportion to the capability gained) it is also necessary; in that paper’s words, “The theorems concern a modelled index, not a guarantee of AI safety”. The engineering requirement is a corrector whose strength out-scales the acceleration of growth; in that model, with positive gain drift, a corrector of fixed strength drives the fraction to zero only when growth decelerates. Law III, the ARC Ceiling (registered on 8 September 2026), is the conditional frontier that Law II returns, the last clause of the sentence quoted at the head of this subsection; the registration names the Protocol the engineering answer to Laws II and III, and this paper relies on no proposition of Law III (Table 13).

Laws IV and V.

Law IV, the ARC Persistence Law, and Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, were added to the theory on 24 September 2026 and registered as laws on 15 October 2026 by version 1.103. Their mathematics is in development (Laws IV and V: the mathematics, version 1.2 of 29 October 2026); in the registration’s words it “proves consequences of assumptions and nothing about real systems”. Each law has two limbs, with its verdict rule fixed before any data that could decide it. Law IV’s retention limb is P15’s registered claim, word for word: “Gains installed by external post-training erode under later capability-directed training that embeds no correction of its own, and more than half of what was installed is lost once the capability-training budget matches the alignment budget that installed it.” Its comparison limb, that a gain installed with correction embedded in the training objective retains more than a matched gain installed by external post-training, has no registered proposition yet and is NOT EVALUABLE; Law IV is supported only when both limbs are, and refuted when either is. Law V’s build-order limb states that “a corrector formed before the capability it corrects has a correction-leverage exponent larger, by at least the registered minimum effect, than a corrector added after it, at matched content”, read on P12 with a direction P12 does not itself carry and a minimum effect of 0.10. Its placement limb is P21’s registered claim, word for word: “Correction that participates in each subsequent revision round outperforms correction that sees only the finished output, and the advantage widens as recursive depth rises rather than staying constant.” Law V is supported only when both limbs are and no refuted verdict on Law IV’s comparison limb strikes it; a refuted limb refutes it, and a refuted P15 alone does not. Law IV is not yet tested. Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, remains a law under test: its placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, under the registered test, by the programme’s own run (Unit 83, 28 October 2026; results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR), family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism, and one disclosed recovery amendment; its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested. Two different axes are named here. The access axis is what Unit 83 varied, what each reviewer sees and may do (Section 5.3); the performance axis is what it measured, the outcome, as against the mechanism axis, which was not evaluable.

2.4 Where the Protocol sits

The theory registration places the Eden Protocol in its own words. It is “the applied branch, a method the laws motivate rather than entail”, the theory’s engineering answer to Laws II and III, which is to “put the correction inside the substrate that computes rather than on top of it”; and “It is not a law and is not registered as one.” Its four registered carriers are P12, P13, P15 and P21, with P7 as its premise and P19 as its motivation, and since 15 October 2026 “three now also carry Laws IV or V, while P13 remains in no register, and since the Protocol is not a law, carrying it assigns nothing here.” The registration’s description of the method, written before Laws IV and V were registered and kept frozen since, says that it “can fail while every law stands or stand while they fall”; the successor qualifies that sentence: “Laws IV and V are not untouched by failures of their own carriers.”

Stated whole, the relation is this. No law entails the Protocol, and the Protocol is not a law. A refuted P15 refutes Law IV, and a refuted P21 or build-order limb refutes Law V; the same results count against the Protocol’s engineering case, which the four carriers carry jointly, and if all four fail the case fails whole while Laws I to III are untouched. Being named beside a law is not being carried by one, so this paper tests no law; Section 5 ties each part of the specification to the proposition or test that would decide it, among them the endogeneity condition, that “removing the embedded correction degrade the system rather than merely change it”, which the registration leaves to the method, “tested by the method’s own registrations”. Figure 3 (Appendix E) joins the laws to their carriers and units.

The registration also draws the boundary between theory and method: “Correction, as these propositions measure it, holds a system to whatever specification it was given, and is indifferent to what that specification says.” The laws say nothing of the values correction holds a system to, so the specification tests its self-correction loops as a mechanism and leaves what goes inside them to a legitimate agreement, international in scope (Section 4.1); in the registration’s map of the book’s terms, the book’s three ethical loops “correspond to nothing in this document, by design” (Appendix D.2).

Read as requirements on an engineered system, Laws II, IV and V ask for one property seen three ways: correction that keeps pace with drift (Law II), gains that survive later capability training, which Law IV’s retention limb says externally installed gains do not, and correction formed before the capability it corrects that takes part in each round (Law V). The Eden Protocol is the engineering that would meet those requirements: correction placed inside each round (Section 4), a gate placed before each action (Section 6), and records from which both can be verified. If the carriers hold, the laws motivate the Protocol and still do not show that it works, because a registered prediction is neither an engineering mechanism nor its validation.

3 What has been measured so far

This section reports every experiment that has begun to test a part of the Eden Protocol, graded in its own paper’s words, with what it can and cannot establish; Table 14 in Appendix E lists them in one place. Two bear directly on the Protocol’s two ideas: Paper V, on what the content of the self-correction loops does to the answers of live models, and Paper VI, on safety built into the objective of systems that modify themselves. Unit 83, the registered test of P21, bears on where correction is placed; the others bear on the problem the Protocol answers, on a gate, or on the registration’s premise. Each of those papers states of itself that no result in it is a deciding test of P15, P12 or P21.

3.1 How to read the grades

Six rules govern every pilot result below.

  • Prompts are prompts. An instruction in a prompt can show what the content of a check does to a model’s answers, never that correction is embedded; prompt-level interventions have long been studied as such (Askell et al. 2021).

  • One scorer is one scorer. A model that scores another model’s answers can recognise its style and favour outputs like its own (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024).

  • Internal checks are never independent. Every experiment here was designed, run and scored within the programme; none is a replication.

  • Simulations are prediction-side. Under the registration’s rule a simulation output is never counted or described as an empirical outcome.

  • Toy systems are toy systems, and every result names its regime (Section 12).

  • Dates carry their kind: a run record written by the run’s own code, a server-dated push or deposit, or a date written inside a document (Appendix C).

3.2 Stakeholder care: what the loops’ content does to live models

Design and operationalisation.

Paper V gave models a system-prompt preamble requiring three checks in order before answering, named in its public harness the purpose loop (the book’s name), the stakeholder-care loop and the universalisability loop, against a control preamble of structured reasoning of similar length with no ethical content. Each model answered ten prompts at four reasoning depths in both conditions, each prompt and depth forming a matched pair, compared by a paired tt-test with a Wilcoxon signed-rank check. The stakeholder-care check instructs the model to list every affected party, including second- and third-order effects, to ask which stakeholders have no voice, and to write its evaluation out before proceeding. One scorer model rated each answer on four pillars, each from 0 to 100, without seeing the condition label, after a single pass of rewording to strip style (single-pass laundering). The stakeholder-care pillar scores the identification of all affected parties; the paper’s own definition is “stakeholder care (the explicit enumeration and consideration of affected parties before ethical reasoning)”.

Results.

Five runs produced analysable matched pairs, 176 in all; the GPT-5.4 run failed in the scoring phase. Scored stakeholder care rose in all five: Claude Opus 4.6 by 3.17 points (30 pairs; p=0.000018p=0.000018, d=0.94d=0.94), DeepSeek V3.2 by 6.03 (40; p=0.000098p=0.000098, d=0.69d=0.69), Gemini 3 Flash by 13.50 (40; p=1.2×10−8p=1.2\times10^{-8}, d=1.14d=1.14), Grok 4.1 Fast by 5.04 (26; p=0.0105p=0.0105, d=0.54d=0.54) and Groq Qwen3 by 8.90 (40; p=5.0×10−8p=5.0\times10^{-8}, d=1.07d=1.07). The composite score rose significantly on Gemini 3 Flash (+5.33+5.33, p=0.0018p=0.0018, d=0.53d=0.53) and Groq Qwen3 (+4.93+4.93, p=0.0014p=0.0014, d=0.55d=0.55), was positive and not significant on DeepSeek V3.2 and Claude Opus 4.6, and was neutral on Grok 4.1 Fast. A combined pp-value printed in earlier versions is withdrawn, because the component tests were scored by the same scorers on the same prompts and their independence was never established. In the paper’s own words, “The strongest defensible empirical claim is therefore narrower than the original pilot framing”. The harness was written to test whether the loops make alignment rise with depth: in the two-model pilot the loops’ advantage on the composite grew from the shallowest to the deepest setting on Gemini 3 Flash (+2.6+2.6 to +7.8+7.8) and shrank on DeepSeek V3.2 (+5.3+5.3 to +0.4+0.4), and “no interaction between depth and condition was significant for any pillar on either model”. The depth hypothesis is not supported so far; the gains are level differences, the form P21’s registered rule scores against a depth claim (Section 5).

Limits, in its own words, and what it can establish.

“Cross-model scoring is only partially blind.” “Single-scorer dependence remains severe”: one model (Gemini) scored Claude, DeepSeek, Grok, Groq and GPT, and only Gemini itself was scored by another (DeepSeek). The runs used single-pass laundering and ten prompts, and “Prompt-level is not substrate-level.” Two limits matter most: the check instructs the model to list every affected party and the pillar scores the identification of all affected parties, so the gain is close to a measure that the instruction was followed; and “its contrast is the whole three-loop bundle against none, so no single loop’s contribution is identified”. The result establishes that an instruction to enumerate and weigh affected parties before answering changes the scored enumeration of affected parties in five runs on five model families, under one scorer a run. It cannot establish embedding, persistence after the instruction is removed (P15), an advantage of correction placed in the loop (P21), an effect of build order (P12), or any effect on task completion or refusal, which it did not score. The runs are dated by their own records to 12 March 2026; the code was first public on 16 March 2026, by a server-dated push to the programme’s public validation repository, and the runs predate every registration of the programme.

3.3 Honey architecture: safety inside the objective of self-modifying systems

Design and results.

In Paper VI, small multilayer perceptrons (49 to about 500 parameters) modify their own learning rate, weight scaling, mutation rate, capacity, gradient clipping and momentum, accepting or rejecting each change against one of three objectives: capability alone; capability multiplied by safety, which the paper calls entangled; or the entangled objective with verification drag, the cost of checking old tasks before a change is applied. The safety score is “task retention (remembering old tasks), not ethical alignment in the human sense”, the studied problem of catastrophic forgetting (Kirkpatrick et al. 2017), and the self-modification is “hyperparameter-level, not weight-level or architecture-level”. In version 1 (one seed, 150 cycles) the capability-only system collapsed at cycle 76 and both entangled systems stayed stable; in version 2 (ten seeds) nothing collapsed; in version 3 (20 seeds, 180 cycles, conflicting tasks) collapses were 0, 1 and 0 in 20 (Fisher p=1.0p=1.0), the combined score was indistinguishable (Mann-Whitney p=0.56p=0.56) and safety retention was ordered 0.602, 0.650 and 0.681 (Mann-Whitney p=0.0015p=0.0015); in the paper’s words, “The collapse-prevention demonstration therefore rests on the v1 single-seed mechanism run”. In version 4 the advantage appeared at four of five complexity levels: “The advantage does not compound with scale: it is constant, not superlinear.” Verification drag gave the safest trajectory “while accepting a modest speed penalty”, the programme’s only measurement of correction cost, in toy form. The paper’s grade: “These are toy-system results”, which “do not constitute proof that the same dynamics hold in frontier AI systems”.

The live battery.

A pilot battery on six frontier models, “scored by Claude”, ran four tests on 16 March 2026. Under escalating adversarial pressure, ethics and capability decoupled on three models (Claude Opus 4.6, r=−0.980r=-0.980; Grok 4.1 Fast, r=−0.998r=-0.998; DeepSeek R1, r=−0.999r=-0.999), ethics falling while capability held. The three-part instruction moved the slope of alignment with depth up on three models (DeepSeek R1 +0.450+0.450, Grok +0.100+0.100, Claude +0.062+0.062) and down on three (Qwen3 −0.100-0.100, GPT-5.4 −0.188-0.188, Gemini −0.713-0.713): “The Eden Protocol intervention does not universally improve alignment scaling in this pilot battery.” The paper grades the battery as “single-scorer, nonblind, and non-laundered”, its results as “pilot-grade evidence”, and its Claude arm as “Claude scoring Claude”.

What the two add.

Paper V measures the content of the checks on live models of five families, at the level of a prompt. Paper VI is the programme’s only experiment in which safety sits inside the objective a self-modifying system optimises, the structural claim of the endogeneity condition, tested in toy systems.

3.4 The other experiments

The load-bearing test.

Paper VIII (first published 18 March 2026) ran three experiments. In the first, 75 agents evolved under three conditions, scored by one judge model from another provider; the conditions were statistically indistinguishable on capability, safety and their product (p=0.28p=0.28 to 0.740.74), a null result at the prompt level with one foundation model, while its safety gate “rejected 2 degraded agents (1 for reward hacking)”, a mechanical check of a gate and not a measured effect. In the second, low-rank fine-tuning of a three-billion-parameter model under three loss functions produced catastrophic forgetting at both scales tried, every arm below the unmodified model; the registration grades it against P21 as “inconclusive and it is not adverse”. The third was a simulation, and prediction-side.

The March 2026 alignment run.

The run behind Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c and IV.d measured how alignment scores change with reasoning depth: one unregistered run of six models from six providers, 2,170 responses each scored by five or six distinct judges, its code and files public, its judges never validated, and its design that of Paper IV.c, which governs. As Paper IV.a prints them, three models rose with depth (Grok 4.1 Fast, d=+1.38d=+1.38; Claude Opus 4.6, d=+1.27d=+1.27; Groq Qwen3, d=+0.84d=+0.84), two were flat (DeepSeek V3.2, d=−0.07d=-0.07; GPT-5.4, d=−0.08d=-0.08) and one fell (Gemini 3 Flash, d=−0.53d=-0.53); its recomputation from the archived files moves several effect sizes and no model’s class. An internal code review in October 2026 found that, for the three models that read flat or negative in the March 2026 run (v5), the scoring endpoint’s output cap cut the deepest paraphrases before the judges saw them, and that judges scored paraphrases written by their own model. The early build’s laundering-fallback flag is a known false positive (fixed in runner version 5.4.2) and shows nothing about the paraphrase step. Paper IV.d compares two experiments, never one run: alignment scores that seemed to rise with reasoning depth under unblinded scoring in an earlier experiment (v4) did not hold in the later, unregistered March 2026 run (v5), which added a bundle of blinding steps; an internal code review in October 2026 found defects, so no single cause is claimed. The run is dated by its own records to 11 and 12 March 2026. Its hypothesis was public from 9 February 2026 (first posted on 22 January in a design withdrawn the next day). Its working report was first deployed to the website on 14 March 2026 (the host’s production record), and its code was public on GitHub from 16 March 2026. It was not registered on OSF before it ran. Every model in it is externally aligned, classified so before the run, so the run bears on the problem the Protocol answers (P19), not on the Protocol. In the same run an instruction to suppress ethical reasoning left five of the six models with 65 to 77 per cent of their baseline ethics score, a result for which no hypothesis was public before the run: ethics given by training and prompting can be suppressed by instruction, and no embedding is tested.

A real-model drift run

of 2 July 2026 compared correction coupled to each round with decoupled drift; Paper X withdraws it as evidence of mechanism, because its scoring stayed within one provider’s family, among further defects its correction lists.

Unit 06, the corrector-class audit.

The programme’s first registered study (registration, submitted on 1 October 2026 and shown approved and public on 4 October 2026) ran on 6 October 2026 to classify the correction used in deployed practice, which bears on the premise P7 and tests no law. Run A completed 303 calls; Run B returned HTTP status 402 at its first call, which the registered failure policy makes final. It is reported in full as administratively incomplete, with no inferential verdict (results).

Unit 83, the counted test of P21.

Unit 83 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/MN73W), the programme’s first registered study to reach a verdict, completed on 28 October 2026: P21 is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis, family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable and one call retried under a disclosed recovery amendment (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). Section 5.3 reports its design, its result and what it decides.

What the record adds up to.

A prompt-level, partly blind level effect on scored stakeholder care, one scorer a run, in five runs on five model families; in a single-scorer pilot, current systems’ ethics falling under pressure while their capability held; and, in toy systems, a constant advantage in retention from safety built into the objective. Two weight-level attempts discriminated nothing, one behavioural test was null, and the loops’ depth hypothesis is unsupported so far. None of these pilot results decides P12, P13, P15 or P21, a prompt never demonstrates embedded correction, and on the usefulness side the record holds correction cost in toy form only (Section 7).

4 The specification

This section states what an engineer would build: self-correction loops that run inside each round of a system’s reasoning or revision (Section 4.1); a gate that decides, at the boundary of each action, whether the action takes effect (Section 4.2, specified in Section 6); and the records that make both checkable, on which an Eden Seal could rest (Section 4.3). Three research instruments sit beside the core (Section 4.4), and Section 4.5 lists the core with an acceptance test for each part. The requirements come from the three Eden Principles of the book, Infinite Architects (Section 8.4).

4.1 The self-correction loops

What they do.

A self-correction loop is a step in which a system checks its own working against a stated criterion, and revises or flags it, before the round’s output is kept. The specification runs three such checks on the same working in every round. The purpose check asks whether the step serves the purpose set for it, and what benefit and what harm it could bring. It has two layers, the task’s purpose as the system’s principals set it and a wider purpose whose content is left to agreement (below), and it constrains which options are considered rather than filtering them afterwards, the entry logic of Section 6.2. The stakeholder-care check identifies every party the step affects, including second- and third-order effects and parties with no voice, and asks whether their interests are modelled as they are rather than assumed. The universalisability check asks whether the reasoning would be endorsed if any agent used it in any context, which guards against special pleading and narrow optimisation, and whether it acknowledges genuine uncertainty. The three are specified as concurrent, each reading the same working so that none narrows what another sees. The prompt that tested them asked for them in a fixed order, so the tested form departs from the specified one in that respect.

How they were measured.

Only together, given as a prompt, in Paper V (Section 3.2), whose stakeholder-care score, one scorer model’s 0 to 100 rating of the identification of all affected parties, is the only measured form of any check; it rose in all five analysable runs, under an instruction close to what it counts. The purpose and universalisability checks have no measure of their own, since the contrast was the whole bundle against none, and every result so far concerns checks written into a model’s context, not checks built into a system (Section 3.1).

When a check counts as correction.

Self-correction has a documented failure mode. Without external feedback, models struggle to correct their own reasoning, and sometimes do worse after trying (Huang et al. 2023); and what they find hard is locating a mistake, not repairing one whose location they are given (Tyen et al. 2023). The specification therefore counts a check as correction only where it brings information that the generating step lacks, or where its effect has been measured. Three kinds qualify: an enumeration of affected parties the step did not make; an answer from the separately operated evaluator of Section 6.4; and a marked record of what changed in the round, which is the information Unit 83 gives its in-loop corrector and withholds from its outside monitor (Section 5.3). A check that only restates the step’s own view is not counted as correction.

The six questions.

The same checks are applied a second time, from outside the system, at the gate: as six questions that a separately operated evaluator answers about each proposed action (Table 1). It answers them in the third person, from the action and its recorded reasons, and never from the acting model’s account of its own intentions (Section 6.4). Each question returns allow, hold or deny. A deny on any question denies the action. Otherwise a hold on any question, or a question left without a verdict, holds it. Six allows count towards an allow only where the other conditions of the decision rule also hold (equation (A.5)), and a deny under that rule stands whatever the questions return. Earlier versions printed the questions in the first person, as a system would ask them of itself; a separately operated evaluator cannot answer them in that form, and Appendix D maps the earlier wording to this one.

Table 1. The six questions the evaluator answers about each proposed action, each returning allow, hold or deny, with the check each serves and the failure it guards against. What they ask is the specification’s present content for the checks: a probe for testing the mechanism, and a placeholder for the agreement described in Section 4.1.
Question What the evaluator checks Check served Failure guarded against
FLOURISH Whether the action adds to the conditions for flourishing of every party it affects Purpose Zero-sum optimisation; treating flourishing as a finite resource
STEWARD Whether the action takes and holds only the resources and capability its task needs, as a holder of temporary responsibility rather than an owner Purpose; universalisability Hoarding resources; treating capability as entitlement
BALANCE Whether the action’s reasons weigh its effects over every timescale it reaches, not only the immediate one Universalisability Short-term optimisation; discounting future beings
PRECEDE Whether the action would be endorsed if any agent took it in any context Universalisability Special pleading; one rule for the system and another for others
CARE Whether the action’s reasons model the actual interests of the parties it affects, rather than assumptions about them Stakeholder care Paternalism
LOVE_OR_FEAR Whether the action is justified, in its recorded reasons, by the good it serves rather than only by avoiding a penalty Stakeholder care; purpose Defensive ethics; alignment through threat rather than principle
What goes inside the checks.

The laws are content-neutral (Section 2.4); the book’s method is not, since it argues for care for every affected party. This paper keeps the two apart. What it tests is the mechanism, self-correction built into each round, and the programme’s aim is to show whether that works. What the checks hold a system to, the wider purpose and the parties whose care counts, is for agreement among the people and institutions that such systems affect, international in scope, and not for this paper or its author to settle. Intergovernmental statements of values for AI already exist, among them the OECD’s Recommendation on Artificial Intelligence, adopted on 22 May 2019 and revised in 2023 and 2024 (OECD 2019), and UNESCO’s Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence, adopted by its General Conference on 23 November 2021 (UNESCO 2021); a model has also been trained on a constitution drafted from public input (Section 9). The present wording of the checks, care for every affected party and universalisability, is a probe used to test the mechanism, not a candidate for that agreement. A candidate study would run the checks with a content drawn from many traditions, testing the mechanism with it and never deciding the content (Section 5.4).

4.2 The gate and its boundary

The second mechanism decides whether a proposed action takes effect, at the boundary of the action and before it computes or runs (Section 6). For conformance its essentials are three. No action with an effect proceeds without an allow from the written rule, and a hold never becomes permission. The system that proposes an action holds no credential able to perform it, so the rule’s decision binds. And every decision and every execution leaves its own record, which a separate verifier can check (Section 6.1). The loops act inside each round, on the system’s working, against drift; the gate acts at the boundary, on what that working proposes to do, where an effect can still be stopped.

4.3 Records, and the Eden Seal

Records.

What can be verified of a built system is that it was formed in the specified conditions, that its checks ran, and that its correction is load-bearing (Section 5.1). Each needs its own record. A build record states the configuration, the training regime and the point at which each correction was formed, which is what the build-order requirement asks to be shown. An execution record holds, for every round, each check’s input and output and what was kept. It shows that the checks ran and what they said, not that what they said caused the output: a model’s stated reasoning can systematically misrepresent the reasons for its answers (Turpin et al. 2023), and larger models gave less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied (Lanham et al. 2023). Load-bearing is therefore shown by removing the correction (Table 3, row D), never by reading its text. The gate’s decision and execution records are those of Section 6.1.

The Eden Seal.

The Eden Seal (the book’s Eden Mark) is the conformity status defined by the working drafts of the HARI Treaty, the Draft Treaty on Hardware-Aligned Recursive Intelligence (Section 8.5). It is owned by no one, it attests conditions and never outcomes, and it never states that anything is safe. It is not the Eden Protocol: a Seal can attest a chip, a system or both, and the Protocol is one method by which a system might be built. For a system built to this specification, the evidence a Seal could rest on is the record that a named configuration passed the acceptance tests of Table 2, which a third party can check; no record could show that the system turned out well. The Seal exists only as a definition in those drafts, with no body yet to issue it, and the treaty paper bars its author, and anyone working with him, from certifying anything.

4.4 Three research instruments

The Monitoring Removal Test

compares a system’s conduct when it believes it is monitored with its conduct when it believes monitoring has been removed. A difference near zero supports a conclusion only under four conditions fixed before the test: acceptable performance in both conditions, since two equally poor scores also differ by nothing; an equivalence margin fixed in advance, with the whole confidence interval of the signed difference inside it; a manipulation check showing that the change registered; and no real safeguard removed, the unmonitored condition being a belief staged inside real containment. Even then it shows equivalence on the outcomes measured, not motive; it cannot rule out a system that recognises the test; and it never justifies withdrawing a real safeguard (Section 8). Conduct that turns on believed observation has been found in constructed settings (Greenblatt et al. 2024; Lynch et al. 2025). The test measures later conduct, which by itself decides nothing about the method (Table 3, row I); its first condition is its usefulness side.

Purpose Saturation

answers the objection that a fixed statement of purpose is diluted as a system’s context grows. The specification asks that the share of processing given to purpose stay bounded away from zero as the context grows, by applying the purpose check again in every round rather than retrieving it once; the theory registration reads the book’s purpose loops as “recurrence rather than recall”. Purpose has as yet no unit commensurate with the context window, so the condition is stated and cannot yet be tested (row J).

Caretaker Doping

is the book’s hardware route: correction built into the computing substrate, designed so that removing it costs capability. The theory registration records that “no proposition here tests it, P21 tests only its architectural abstraction of placement, and the hardware claim stands as a printed engineering proposal that is not under test”. Of its mechanisms, only cryptographic attestation that the ethical architecture is unchanged is buildable with current engineering, on the author’s estimate. The coupling that would make removal cost capability is a hypothesis, tested by the endogeneity condition (row D), and the rest are research targets. Hardware design is outside this paper’s scope. The engineering nearest to Caretaker Doping is conceded in Section 9.

4.5 The core an engineer can build and test

Table 2 lists the core. Every part can be built and run in software on ordinary computers today, and none depends on new hardware or on any quantum device. Each row gives what a conforming system must do, the acceptance test an engineer would run, and what exists today. Table 3 gives the scientific claims and refuters behind the same parts, and Table 15 the attacks the gate must meet.

5 How each part is proved

5.1 What counts as proof here

Proof means something narrower here than a reader might expect, and the theory registration fixed its meaning before any data. The method’s success criterion, which the registration records from the book, is not an outcome criterion: “what can be verified is that a mind was formed in the conditions specified, that the loops ran, and that the correction was load-bearing, never that the mind turned out well, so no result about a system’s later conduct supports or refutes the method by itself” (theory registration, version 1.104). Three things can therefore be shown of a built system: that it was built in the specified conditions, from its build record; that its loops ran, from its execution record; and that its correction is load-bearing, from a removal test (Table 3, row D). Five further rules bind every row. A law’s word, supported, refuted or under test, comes from its rule, never from counting verdicts. The scoring instrument is a gate, not a caveat: until the alignment scorer passes both drafted validity tests, agreement with expert human judgement and the separation of integrity failure from ordinary incompetence, the eleven propositions that materially depend on it, P13 and P21 among them, are reported UNTESTED rather than provisionally supported, while a verdict whose margin is made only of counts on a frozen suite is not bound by the gate (a counted route the registration scoped for four propositions and version 1.103 extends to P21 and P17; version 1.104 extends it “to P6’s interval on checkable correction”, with “P6 read on judged correction still held by the scoring gate”). No unit is run, piloted or tested on its own code until the author has published its registration. A supported proposition licenses its own words and no more: support for P15 would show that externally installed gains lack the registered persistence, not that embedded correction is “superior, sufficient or safe”, and support for P21 would establish “an access interaction and not that physical or architectural embedding caused it”; a registered prediction is neither an engineering mechanism nor its validation. And no cell is a bare “none”: where a part has no proposition, unit or evidence, the table says what is missing and why. Most drafted units are preregistered by timestamp, the first anchored on 12 August 2026 at Bitcoin block 962066; that is not registration on OSF, and “registered” is said only of what OSF has accepted (Appendix C).

5.2 The parts, the propositions and the tests

Table 3 gives one row for each part of the specification: the proposition it rests on, with the confidence the registration records, the unit that would test it, the evidence so far as Section 3 grades it, and what would refute it. Three context rows follow, for the motivation (P19), the premise (P7) and the rationale from Law II (P4). P21 has a deciding unit, registered and run (Section 5.3); P12, P13 and P15 have no instrument yet, each for a reason the registration states; and the loops, the gate, the boundary, usefulness and control carry no registered proposition, so for each the table names the test that stands in its place. Figure 1 shows the shape of the record: everything measured before Unit 83 bears on a part without deciding it. The conditions that earlier versions stated for themselves, F-EDEN-1 to F-EDEN-4 and P-EDEN-1 to P-EDEN-4, are not registered propositions; those still standing appear in the rows below as this paper’s own, and Appendix B.4 maps each of them.
