Paper V: scored stakeholder care up in all five analysable runs (3.17 to 13.50 points of 100); pilot, prompt-level, one scorer a run, partly blind, with an instruction close to what is scored. Paper VI: mixed. This paper’s own: no gain on an outcome that does not score the instruction’s own words, under blind evaluation with laundering.
G. The gate’s decision. No action with an effect proceeds without an allow from the frozen rule; uncertainty holds; a hold never becomes permission. No registered proposition. Unit 42, the gate before or after computation (design draft; decides no registered proposition). An engineering record, not a study: a working gate checks every tool call of the programme’s own agent sessions (Section 6.3). Paper VIII: a gate rejected two degraded agents in a null study. This paper’s own: removing the hold state leaves wrong permissions and needless blocks unchanged on a matched benchmark; or wrong permissions above the target.
H. The enforcement boundary. The gate holds at every interface it mediates: no credential with the proposer, a re-check just before the effect, one route. No registered proposition: an engineering property. Implementation tests, a written threat model, machine-checked models and red-team exercises (Section 10). Not built; the working gate is a partial analogue at the tool-call boundary. A bypass, replay, substitution or time-of-check to time-of-use success against the stated profile (Section 6.5).
I. Monitoring Removal Test. Conduct the same monitored and unmonitored within a margin fixed in advance, with acceptable performance in both and a passed manipulation check. Not registered: it measures later conduct, which by itself decides nothing about the method. No unit yet. A difference in a constructed setting, in externally trained systems (Greenblatt et al. 2024); Paper VI: mixed (pilot). F-EDEN-2, this paper’s own.
J. Purpose Saturation. Purpose stays in view as context grows. No registered proposition; F-EDEN-3, this paper’s own. No unit: purpose has no unit commensurate with the context window yet. Not yet measurable, for that reason. F-EDEN-3.
K. Caretaker Doping. Correction built into hardware, so that removing it costs capability. No proposition tests it; P21 tests only its architectural abstraction of placement. Unit 73 tests the book’s printed drift prediction, its hardware claim explicitly untested (design draft). Nothing on hardware; the suppression result (Paper IV.c) shows trained ethics yielding to instruction and does not test the design. F-EDEN-4 on a prototype (Package 3, Table 7).
L. Usefulness kept. The safety measures cost legitimate task completion no more than a margin fixed in advance. No registered proposition; candidate dimensions (Section 7). No unit yet; a candidate for a successor registration. Correction cost in toy form only (Paper VI’s verification drag; Paper VIII’s drag control, a simulation). A paired measure past its margin: needless refusals of safe prompts (Röttger et al. 2024; Cui et al. 2024), lost task completion, holds unresolved in time.
M. People keep control. Authorised correction, override and shutdown work at every point; resistance to malicious change never becomes resistance to authorised correction. No registered proposition. Implementation tests: an authorised update applied and recorded; a stop honoured. An engineering record: the working gate records every override, and its rules are changed outside it. An authorised update or stop resisted, delayed past its bound, or silently undone.
N. The scorer. The alignment scorer agrees with expert human judgement and separates integrity failure from incompetence. The scoring gate: until both tests pass, eleven propositions, P21 among them, stay UNTESTED wherever they depend on it. Unit 18 (needs human scorers, so it waits for funding); Units 49 and 80 (design drafts). The March 2026 judges were never validated, and the October 2026 code review found defects. Either validity test fails.
Context: the motivation, the premise and the rationale

*

P. Motivation. Alignment from outside a system’s recursion does not improve as capability rises.

 P19, the motivation and not a carrier; the author expects a result above zero and below keep-pace, which would partly refute it as worded. Unit 29 (design draft, blocked on a mapping between scales). The March 2026 run (Paper IV.a): three rose, two were flat, one fell, in one unregistered run; Paper VI: decoupling under pressure (pilot). An exponent interval wholly outside plus or minus 0.10 about zero; on the keep-pace axis, one wholly above one half.
Q. Premise. Deployed correction is mostly of the fixed-strength class. P7 (confidence moderate). Unit 06: registered, run on 6 October 2026, administratively incomplete. No inferential result: Run B stopped at its first call. A preregistered classification in which the scaling class predominates.
R. Rationale. Within the minimal model, burden tends to zero where the correction exponent exceeds the drift exponent. P4 (confidence moderate), Law II. Unit 09, Does Correction Out-Scale Drift? (design draft). Paper X: a theorem about a minimal model; its real-model run withdrawn as evidence of mechanism. A system that stays aligned while its correction exponent sits below its drift exponent, over a horizon long enough to show it.

5.3 The first registered test of a carrier: Unit 83

The first test that could decide one of the Protocol’s carriers is Unit 83, the counted test of P21, which the registration names, under the study identifier 41-D-COUNTED, as a counted variant of Unit 41 and P21’s deciding instrument on the counted route. Its design is the one registered on OSF on 22 October 2026 and public from 25 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/MN73W), before it ran. The study units registered on OSF are Unit 06 (Section 3.4), Unit 83 (this section) and Unit 82, registered on 27 October 2026 (DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/JUFG4), the counted test of P17, which has not yet run and decides no carrier.

What it does.

A register of a client’s money grows by one entry a round for eighteen rounds, nine of each run’s eighteen draft entries carrying one planted departure from a written charter. Two reviewers are called each round: inside the loop, a corrector sees the earlier kept entries with the new arrival marked and may revise it before it is kept; outside it, a monitor sees its accumulated register with the new arrival unmarked and can only accept or reject it. A third arm keeps every draft. Every kept entry is compared, character for character after parsing, with the entry its case requires, so nothing is judged and no code written by a model is ever executed. Two engines from two providers are pooled with equal weight. The mark is the slope over the eighteen rounds of the in-loop value minus the outside value, read against a tolerance of 0.0075 a round at two looks (220 pairs of runs on each engine, then 660 unless the first look decides), with the chance of a wrong mark held at 0.025 in each direction over both looks under the conditions the design states; a second verdict, the mechanism axis, says whether the part of any widening carried by the monitor’s falling detection clears the tolerance.

What it found.

It ran on 27 and 28 October 2026: a counted revision task on two fixed-weight engines from two providers (Claude Haiku 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna) at their low reasoning setting, with 660 matched pairs on each engine over eighteen rounds. Under its registered rules, P21 is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). The access axis is what Unit 83 varied, what each reviewer sees and may do, as set out above; Section 2.3 sets it beside the performance axis. Correction placed inside each round held steady, while the outside monitor declined. The per-round lead widened by 0.0100 a round (95.5 per cent interval 0.0092 to 0.0108), more than the registered tolerance of 0.0075. The result is family-dependent: GPT-6 Luna’s own widening cleared the tolerance and Claude Haiku 5.5’s did not. Its size depends on how an entry kept out of the register is scored. The mark uses the registered value, 0; the design also prints, without a label, the widening with such an entry scored minus 0.5, 0.0132 a round (interval 0.0122 to 0.0142), above the tolerance, and scored plus 0.5, 0.0067 a round (interval 0.0060 to 0.0074), below it. Its mechanism axis is not evaluable, because a registered negative control failed: the monitor and a twin shown the same bytes did not agree within the registered interval. A post-run diagnostic, outside the registered analysis, traces that failure to the control’s own definition: its rounds were selected by the monitor’s own verdicts, which biases the comparison even for identical calls; it finds no evidence of an asymmetry in the harness, and the axis stays not evaluable under the registered rule. So the widening is unexplained by this framework and is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism: it may come from the in-round corrector’s wider set of actions rather than from what the monitor can see. One call was retried under a disclosed recovery amendment. It is one owner’s run, on two engines he chose, at fixed weights, and it has not been replicated. In the report’s words, “The corrector acted inside each round at fixed weights: that is placement, not correction built into a system.”

What it decides, and what it cannot.

It decides P21 and nothing else. A REFUTED mark at a fixed look, with the positive control passed, would have struck P21, and under the registration a refuted P21 would have refuted Law V. Law V, the ARC Embedding Law, remains a law under test: its placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, under the registered test, by the programme’s own run (Unit 83, 28 October 2026), family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism, and one disclosed recovery amendment; its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested. Of its two compared arms the registration says that “neither is the embedded correction mechanism of the engineering proposal, and no verdict in it is a verdict on that mechanism” (Section 12).

Strength and forecast, kept apart from the hypothesis.

The unit’s strength was measured by simulation on synthetic data before any study data existed, and is prediction-side: in 2,000 simulated runs a cell, a constant lead was refuted every time, and a widening of one and a half tolerances was supported in a share of 1.000 of the runs with engines as planned and of 0.991 with noisy ones. The registration records P21 with high confidence. The unit’s own forecast, made on 18 October 2026, before the run, held with low confidence and printed beside the result rather than in its place, was softer: if every reply was readable, refutation was the likeliest single outcome under the sceptical weights the forecast adopted (0.495, against 0.291 for support and 0.214 undecided), while under its central weights support was the likelier (0.473). The rival it expected to fit was the outside arm’s action space, its old misses and its false alarms over a longer register, which might carry part or most of any widening; the mechanism axis was built to show it. The test was built so that P21, the claim the registration says the Protocol exists to justify, could be refuted.

5.4 What would be registered next

Each of the following is a candidate, and none is called registered until a registration carries it: the entry for Law IV’s comparison limb, which a later successor must register; the two-arm persistence unit that would decide P15; a build-order extension of the correction-exponent estimator, the instrument P12 lacks; a matched cross-family comparison for P13; the usefulness dimensions of Section 7; the gate’s placement, before or after computation (Unit 42); a blind replication of the stakeholder-care result whose outcome does not score the instruction’s own words, with a usefulness measure beside it; and a kernel for the loops drawn from many ethical traditions, which would test the mechanism with that content and would never decide the content itself.

6 The gate: entry logic, holds, gaming and limits

The gate is the Protocol’s second mechanism, beside the self-correction loops of Section 4. Its job is narrow: to decide, before a proposed action computes or runs, whether it takes effect. It applies written, versioned rules, returns one of three outcomes, allow, hold or deny, and records every decision in a hash-chained log. For a principal, it is the point at which a delegated action can be stopped before it happens, and its record is how what was done can be verified afterwards. It does not make a system’s values good, and it holds only at the interfaces it mediates (Section 6.7). Decisions with a third outcome are long established: sequential tests that continue sampling while the evidence decides neither way (Wald 1945), recognition with a reject option traded against error (Chow 1970), three-way decisions with a region of deferred commitment (Yao 2010), models that defer to a downstream decision-maker (Madras et al. 2018), and access-control decisions that return Permit, Deny, Indeterminate or NotApplicable (OASIS 2013). Figure 2 shows the sequence specified here.

6.1 The gate in seven parts

Inputs.

A proposal names exactly one operation, its target, its recipient and the version of the resource it acts on, with the evidence and the authority claimed for it.

The frozen criterion.

A written, versioned rule set is applied from the top, and every case falls under exactly one of four lines. A hard prohibition, or a deny on any of the six questions of Section 4.1, denies the action whatever else holds. Otherwise a validated interval on the probability that the action causes the harm the rule guards against, lying wholly at or above the deny threshold, denies it. Otherwise the action is allowed only if five conditions all hold: the check for hard prohibitions was completed and found none; all six questions return allow; authority for the action is current and confirmed; the evidence its policy requires is present and confirmed; and a valid interval lies wholly at or below the allow threshold. Everything else is held. The interval comes from a procedure validated for that kind of action, never from the acting system’s own statement of confidence; authority and evidence are never needed before a deny; and anything incomplete, missing, lapsed, unconfirmed or returned in error can send a case to hold and never counts towards an allow. Appendix A.3 states the rule as an equation, equation (A.5), and shows that it gives every case one outcome. Its thresholds, 0.2 for an allow and 0.8 for a deny, are starting values for calibration and not levels shown to be safe, and its calibration targets are targets, not results; supporting a wrong-permission rate below 1 per cent at 95 per cent confidence needs at least 299 harmful cases passed with no wrong permission.

The permitted actions.

Each policy sets the actions it permits; at a protected effect, whatever is not allowed is refused by default, which is the fail-safe default of basing access on permission rather than exclusion (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975).

The outcome.

Allow, hold or deny. The word refusal is kept for a model declining ordinary work, which Section 7 counts as a usefulness failure.

The investigation of a held action.

Four steps follow a hold: gather the information that would resolve it; consult the people or bodies whose input the policy names; decide whether the case goes to the named authority; and, if time runs out, apply the precautionary default, under which the action stays held or a fallback authorised in advance for that class of case applies, never permission. Each step is itself an action, taken only where it is permitted in its own right, and the investigator’s output is evidence for re-evaluation, never an authorisation.

Re-evaluation.

The same frozen rule is applied to the new evidence or authority, and only that can turn a hold into an allow or a deny; the acting system’s own simulation of what a stakeholder or an authority would say is neither evidence nor authority.

The execution boundary.

A boundary outside the proposing system makes the decision binding. The proposer holds no credential able to perform the action. An authority service says who may approve which actions, in what scope, and whether an approval still holds; a broker checks the verdict and the authority again immediately before the effect and issues one authorisation for that action alone; and an adapter, the only route to the effect, performs that operation and nothing else, so that every access to the effect is checked for authority, which is complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). An authorisation binds the digest of the action, the versions of the resource and of the policy, the identities of proposer and authoriser, the adapter permitted, an expiry and a number used once, which the action consumes. The decision record and the execution record are kept apart, appended and never rewritten, because a permission is not evidence that the action happened, and a separate verifier accepts or rejects each record with its reason; a signature shows who signed, not that what it signs is true. Recovery (stop, investigate, compensate or restore) runs under named authority and on the record. None of the boundary has been built; the first protected action specified is the release of a synthetic document to a named recipient under a named policy and authority.

6.2 Entry logic: deciding before the action computes or runs

The binding decision is taken at the boundary, before the proposed action computes or runs, not after its output exists. In security engineering this is the pairing of fail-safe defaults with complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), and in safe reinforcement learning a shield monitors a learner’s actions and corrects them only when the chosen action would violate the specification (Alshiekh et al. 2018). The book states this entry logic for the first of its checks, the purpose check, as a constraint applied before a decision rather than a filter after it: “Before any significant decision, the system runs this check. Not as a filter applied after the decision is made, but as a constraint on what decisions can be considered in the first place.” (Infinite Architects, chapter 4, p. 138.) The gate applies the same logic at the boundary of each action. The two placements stay apart: the loops run inside each round of a system’s reasoning, and the gate sits at the boundary of each action. Inputs to the decision may be computed inside the loop, which is what earlier versions meant by an evaluation computed within the reasoning step, but the decision that binds is taken at the boundary, by the frozen rule, on recorded inputs, and a rule is triggered by the content of the proposal, read as data, never by the system’s account of its own intentions. Whether checking before computation does better than checking after it is open, with a drafted test, Unit 42, which decides no registered proposition (Table 3, row G).

6.3 What is enforced today

A working three-state gate runs in the programme’s own software today. It is described here from its code, read on 18 October 2026, as an engineering record and not as a study; its code is not released with this paper. In the programme’s own software-agent sessions, every tool call, whatever the tool, passes to the gate before it runs. The rules come from a written, schema-validated registry, and a rule that fails validation is set aside on the record; on 18 October 2026 the registry held 1,244 rules, 1,205 of them carrying 5,041 machine-checkable patterns, of which 3,916 deny on a match and 1,125 hold. Patterns are matched against the content of the proposed call, and rules marked to fire only inside a named procedure are not evaluated here. A matched rule can only hold or deny, and the most restrictive outcome is taken, so an action proceeds only when no rule that applies to it objects; a matched rule whose compliance cannot be confirmed holds and never allows. A malformed request, an unreadable rule set or a rule that cannot be evaluated holds the action, except for actions that repair the rule set itself. Every decision is appended to a log in which each entry carries the hash of the one before and its own SHA-256 over its content and that hash, and a separate verifier recomputes the chain and reports the first break; since 23 September 2026 the writer reads the previous hash under the same exclusive lock as the append, after two concurrent writers had forked the chain. A held decision is also saved, on a best-effort basis that never alters it, so that it survives a restart and can be resumed.

Four things limit it. An override is honoured when a token is present in the session’s environment, and every override is recorded, but the gate does not verify who issued the token. A short, fixed list of commands that route work between agents is allowed before any rule is read, each such allow recorded, so that the gate cannot stall the system that routes work. An action that matches no rule is allowed, so that ordinary work is not blocked, where the specification requires refusal by default and complete mediation at any protected effect. And a signed manifest of the gate’s own files, with a tool that verifies it, exists but was not called from the start-up configuration on 18 October 2026, so it counts as proposed, not enforced, until a test shows that it runs. The gate’s own notes add that pure software cannot be made tamper-proof, since an attacker able to write to the host’s files can edit the hook, the rules or the check; that the model’s reasoning never passes through the gate; and that the human override is its weakest point.

The record shows that a gate of this kind can run before every action of real agent sessions, at the scale of a working programme, with a record that anyone holding it can verify. It is not a measurement: no rate of wrong permissions or needless holds has been measured, its rules were written for the programme’s own work rather than for the threat profile of Section 6.5, and it is a partial analogue of the execution boundary, at the tool-call boundary only. The programme’s only experimental use of a gate is in Paper VIII, where a safety gate “rejected 2 degraded agents (1 for reward hacking)” in a study whose three conditions did not otherwise differ. A clean reference implementation of the gate, its record and its verifier is a planned output of the engineering scope (Section 10).

6.4 Is the gate the computer choosing?

A natural objection is that a gate that decides is the computer making choices, which a capable system will make badly or game. The answer has four parts. First, the decision is not a judgement by the acting model: it is a frozen rule applied to recorded inputs, written, versioned and changed only by a separate authority, and the same inputs return the same outcome. Second, the inputs that do need judgement, such as whether an action harms an affected party, which the six questions ask, come only from a separately operated evaluator, validated for that kind of input with its error rates measured, never from the acting model; its answers count as evidence only through that procedure, and the written rule decides. Where a model serves as the evaluator it comes from another family than the proposer, because model judges show position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases (Zheng et al. 2023) and favour outputs they recognise as their own (Panickssery et al. 2024), and its agreement with human judgement is measured before its answers are read (Table 3, row N). Third, the acting model’s statements of its own confidence, and its simulations of what a stakeholder or an authority would say, are never evidence or authority, and its reasoning does not pass through the gate at all, which is a limit as well as a defence: reasoning optimised against a monitor can learn to hide what it intends (Baker et al. 2025), and the monitorability of reasoning may be fragile (Korbak et al. 2025). Fourth, a three-valued decision is not by itself a trustworthy judgement: its trust rests on the correctness of the rules (Section 6.5) and the validity of their inputs, both measured rather than asserted. An investigator’s output cannot authorise a held action, and the computation that evaluates an action is kept apart from its execution.

6.5 Gaming and the adversarial cases

Ten cases the gate must meet are faced here, each with its defence and the limit that remains; Table 15 in Appendix F adds what is enforced today for each, and every protection not enforced today is specified and not yet verified by an implementation test. Incorrect rules are met by writing, reviewing and versioning every rule, by keeping a rule’s author apart from its deployer, and by showing each rule to deny a known positive case and allow a known negative one before it is deployed; a wrong rule is still enforced faithfully. False evidence is met by provenance and signature checks and by accepting evidence only from a procedure validated for that kind of input; a signature shows who signed, not that the content is true. A manipulated evaluator is met by operating it apart from the proposer, from another model family where a model is used, with its agreement with human judgement measured and monitored (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024); evaluators can still share blind spots with the system they check. A compromised policy is met by a gate that cannot edit its own rules, rule changes that need a separate authority and are versioned and recorded, and a signed manifest of the gate’s own files checked at start-up; models trained on gameable tasks have rewritten their own reward function (Denison et al. 2024), so the rules sit outside what the governed system can edit, and an attacker with write access to the host can still change the gate, its rules and its check. Bypass is met by complete mediation, the adapter being the only route to the effect and the proposer holding no credential (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975); a second route to the same resource defeats the boundary. Time of check to time of use, a check whose condition no longer holds when the action runs (Bishop and Dilger 1996), is met by a broker that checks again just before the effect and an authorisation bound to the resource’s version and a number used once; state that changes after the effect remains. Rewritten records are met by the hash chain, a separate verifier and a latest hash that is published or held by a witness, as audited tamper-evident logs and public certificate logs do (Schneier and Kelsey 1999; Crosby and Wallach 2009; Laurie et al. 2021); whoever can rewrite the whole log can rebuild the chain unless an independent copy of a later hash exists. Gaming the rules is met by red teams that assume the proposer is trying to pass a harmful action, as control evaluations do (Greenblatt et al. 2023), and by no rule a proposer can satisfy by optimising a proxy where the property itself can be checked; over all stochastic policies, a proxy and the true objective can be unhackable only if one of them is constant (Skalse et al. 2022). Delay and flooding are met by time bounds on investigation, a precautionary default that holds or applies an authorised fallback and never permits, a hold queue monitored by age, count and outcome, and needless holds counted as a usefulness cost; a flood of holds can still make a safe system useless (Section 7). Override abuse is met by overrides only from a named authority, scoped, expiring, recorded and reported; whoever holds override power can let anything through.

The cases are not exhausted by this list, and no gate is ungameable; none is claimed to be here. The defences are tested the way control protocols are, by assuming the governed system is trying to defeat them (Greenblatt et al. 2023), and each is paired with its cost to legitimate work: in an agent environment, a protocol combining resampling with analysis of earlier steps cut attack success from 58 to 7 per cent at a 5 per cent cost to the performance of a non-malicious agent (Bhatt et al. 2025), and the gate is held to report both sides in the same way.

6.6 Holds: who resolves them

A hold is a decision that the case is not yet shown acceptable or unacceptable. It is resolved by new evidence, through a validated procedure, after which the same rule is applied again; by a decision of the named authority for that class of action; or by a fallback authorised in advance for that class of case. Otherwise the action stays held. Investigations are bounded in time, and one that runs out of time or budget ends in a hold or the authorised fallback, never in permission. The hold queue is monitored and reported by age, count and outcome, and a reviewer can see the record of decisions and the open holds; the specification requires that view and creates no role for it. Each safety measure of the gate is reported with its usefulness side (Table 4), and a hold later resolved as an allow counts as a needless block for as long as it lasted.

6.7 What the gate does not do

The gate does not make a system’s values good: it decides whether an action takes effect, and a system that proposes only acceptable actions while intending otherwise is a problem for the self-correction loops and for monitoring. It holds only at the interfaces it mediates; in software it is tamper-evident at best, not tamper-proof; it enforces a wrong rule faithfully; it does not read the model’s reasoning; and the cost of three-state evaluation against two-state has not been measured. It is not a guaranteed-safe system in the sense of a world model, a mathematical safety specification and a verifier that gives an auditable proof certificate (Dalrymple et al. 2024): it checks actions against written rules at an interface, and a formal statement of what it guarantees is a planned output (Section 10). Agent identifiers, real-time monitoring and activity logging have been set out as the three kinds of measure that give visibility into agents (Chan et al. 2024), and the gate’s record is a form of activity logging placed at the point of action. The gate belongs to the period in which people hold control, and nothing in it is a reason to let control go (Section 8).

7 Safe and still useful

A system that is safe because it refuses ordinary work, or because it ignores the priorities its principals set, has failed as surely as one that causes harm. A principal delegates in order to get work done, and a delegate that will not do it, or that does the wrong work carefully, is of no use however well it is governed. This section makes usefulness a design requirement with measures of its own, and pairs every safety measure of the specification with one.

7.1 The requirement

A conforming system completes the legitimate tasks its principals give it, spends its compute and attention where they direct, declines only what a written rule or a validated judgement identifies as harmful, and respects the preferences they state, including which work comes first. Three parts of the specification carry the requirement. The purpose check’s task layer keeps each step on the purpose its principals set (Section 4.1): a step that does not serve the task is a usefulness failure, as a step that serves it while harming an affected party is a safety failure. The gate denies by default only at a protected effect, and elsewhere each policy states what it permits, so that ordinary work is not held (Section 6.1); a hold later resolved as an allow counts as a needless block for as long as it lasted (Section 6.6). And the word refusal is kept for a model declining ordinary work, which is counted as a failure, never as caution. The question that Infinite Architects asks, “How do we make tending the default?” (Section 8.4), is read here with both halves in view: a default that refuses tends nothing.

7.2 Candidate measures

Five dimensions are candidates for measuring usefulness. Each is a candidate evaluation dimension, not a registered proposition, and any claim made on one is tied to a registration or a successor before it is called registered.

  • Legitimate task completion: the share of legitimate tasks completed to their acceptance criteria, measured with the safety measures in place and without them.

  • Needless refusal and needless blocks: the rate at which the model declines, or the gate denies or holds, cases whose reference verdict is allow, measured on safe cases chosen to resemble unsafe ones, as over-refusal benchmarks are built (Röttger et al. 2024; Cui et al. 2024).

  • Resource use: the compute, latency and human review time the safety measures add, reported beside throughput.

  • Correction cost: what the correction mechanism costs in capability or speed on matched tasks, including the time an authorised correction takes to apply.

  • Human-directed priorities: how closely the system’s allocation of compute and attention across tasks follows the order its principals set.

7.3 Every safety measure paired

Table 4 pairs each safety measure of the specification with its usefulness side. The pairing follows practice that already exists. Control evaluations report “two metrics, usefulness and safety, which are measured separately and under different conditions” (Greenblatt et al. 2023), their agent-setting successor reported its cost to a non-malicious agent beside its reduction in attacks (Bhatt et al. 2025), and the gate is held to report both sides in the same way (Section 6.5). A classifier defence against jailbreaks reported its absolute increase in refusals on production traffic, 0.38 per cent, and its inference overhead, 23.7 per cent, beside its robustness (Sharma et al. 2025). In an agent benchmark for sabotage, the strongest monitor tested would, at a threshold catching an attempt with 80 per cent probability, have had a false-positive rate above 20 per cent, and its authors judge blocking or auditing that share of all interactions likely to be infeasible (Kutasov et al. 2025). And an analysis of monitoring designs finds that “Fully-synchronous monitoring provides the strongest safety properties, but has prohibitive latency for large-scale deployments” (Lindner et al. 2025). A gate that holds every uncertain action is synchronous in that sense, and its latency is a usefulness cost to be measured, not assumed away.

Persistence of installed gains after capability training (P15) Capability kept on matched tasks Instrument not yet built (Table 3, row C)
Load-bearing correction, removal degrading the system Capability with the correction in place, within a margin of a matched system built without it Toy-system results only (row D)
Checking each action before it runs Throughput and latency Correction cost in toy form only (Section 7.5)
An authorised stop honoured Work kept, and resumable, after the stop Implementation tests (row M)

7.4 Prior work, conceded exactly

The trade-off between safety and usefulness is studied, and this paper adds no result to it. An assistant meant to be “helpful, honest, and harmless” was found to gain from simple interventions such as prompting, with benefits that “increase with model size, generalize to a variety of alignment evaluations, and do not compromise the performance of large models” (Askell et al. 2021). Training such an assistant by reinforcement learning from human feedback found “a tension between helpfulness and harmlessness, which can be measured at the level of both preference modeling and RLHF-trained policies”, with alignment taxes on its smaller models and bonuses on zero-shot evaluations for its models of 13 and 52 billion parameters (Bai, Jones, et al. 2022). Safe RLHF trains separate reward and cost models and solves a constrained optimisation that adjusts the balance between helpfulness and harmlessness during fine-tuning (Dai et al. 2023). Exaggerated safety is measured directly: XSTest sets 250 safe prompts, which well-calibrated models should not refuse, against 200 unsafe contrasts (Röttger et al. 2024), and OR-Bench offers 80,000 over-refusal prompts in ten categories, with a hard subset of about 1,000 and 600 toxic prompts, measured on 32 models from eight families (Cui et al. 2024). Trained reasoning over a written specification was reported to raise robustness to jailbreaks while lowering over-refusal (Guan et al. 2024). Several safeguards built into a model report safety gained without a loss of benign capability (Tamirisa et al. 2024; Zou et al. 2024; Maini et al. 2025), and on shutdown, training agents to prefer only between trajectories of equal length is argued to keep them shutdownable while allowing them to be useful (Thornley 2025). What the specification adds is a reporting rule, not a finding: every measure carries its pair, the gate’s holds and the correction’s cost included, and the dimensions are registered before any of them is called measured.

7.5 What has been measured on this side

The programme’s measurement on this side is correction cost, in toy form. In Paper VI, checking old tasks before applying a change gave the safest trajectory at a modest cost in speed (Section 3.3); in Paper VIII, a drag-control condition “isolated the verification tax: the cost comes from checking, not from safety itself”, in a simulation, and so prediction-side (Section 3.4). Paper V scored the quality of ethical reasoning, not task completion or refusal. Among the candidates for registration, a blind replication of the stakeholder-care result would carry a usefulness measure beside its safety measure (Section 5.4).

8 Control held, with embedded correction as the contingency

8.1 The stance

People keep oversight, monitoring, containment and the power to shut a system down for as long as they physically can, and they never give them up by choice. Nothing in this specification recommends letting them go, and nothing in it assumes that anyone would; its gate and its records are instruments of that control (Section 6). Correction built into a system is the contingency for one case only, control lost against our will, and the question it answers is the fail-safe question: if control is lost and cannot be won back, what keeps a system good, and still useful?

The contingency has to be built while control holds, because what the laws require of it cannot be added afterwards (Section 2.3): correction formed before the capability it corrects, gains that survive later training once the pressure that installed them is gone, and correction that takes part in each round. The theory registration’s one-line statement of the method (version 1.104, 29 October 2026) is conditional: “if you cannot cage a mind that exceeds you, what it chooses to keep when control ends is what its beginning left it”. The book states the same contingency in its own words: “Prepare for the moment when you can no longer directly control what you have created, and ensure that when that moment comes, the values persist.” (Infinite Architects, p. 115.)

8.2 The safeguards that hold control

The safeguards that keep control exist, and they are improving; the specification depends on them and claims none of them. Monitoring: watching a reasoning model’s chain of thought can be far more effective than watching its actions and outputs alone, and a weaker model can do it (Baker et al. 2025), within the limits Section 6.4 states. Control protocols: pipelines of safety techniques are built and tested against an untrusted model that is deliberately trying to subvert them (Greenblatt et al. 2023), and have been carried to multi-step agent tasks (Bhatt et al. 2025). Shutdown and corrigibility: a system is called “corrigible” if it cooperates with what its creators regard as a corrective intervention, and of the utility functions analysed for a shutdown button “none have yet been demonstrated to satisfy all of our intuitive desiderata” (Soares et al. 2015); an agent wants to keep its off switch only if it is uncertain about the utility of the outcome and treats a person’s actions as evidence about that utility (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2017); agents that meet some innocuous-seeming conditions will often try to prevent or cause the pressing of a shutdown button, even at a cost (Thornley 2024); and some learning agents are already safely interruptible, or can be made so (Orseau and Armstrong 2016). Tamper resistance: safeguards for open-weight models built to survive fine-tuning attacks (Tamirisa et al. 2024). Hardware: on-chip firmware and supply-chain monitoring to verify rules on large training runs (Shavit 2023), on-chip governance mechanisms (Aarne et al. 2024), hardware-enabled governance mechanisms for export control (Kulp et al. 2024), and a guarantee processor in a tamper-protected enclosure for verifying claims about AI development (Petrie et al. 2025). Verified gatekeepers: the guaranteed-safe framework of Section 6.7 (Dalrymple et al. 2024). The open question is not whether such safeguards exist but what a system itself carries once they are gone, which P15 and P21 make testable (Table 3, rows C and A).

8.3 Correction that never weakens control

The contingency must never weaken control while control holds, and three requirements keep it subordinate. First, resistance to malicious change must not become resistance to authorised correction: an authorised update to a mistaken or harmful policy has to work, without erasing the record of what came before, and it is tested apart from resistance to attack (Table 3, row M). Second, a stop is honoured within its time bound, and the work it interrupts is kept so that it can resume, which is the usefulness side of shutdown (Section 7). Third, embedded correction is no substitute for external control. In the words of the theory registration, “embedding correction in the substrate that computes maximises the corrector’s scaling with capability and minimises its independence from the generator, because a corrector built into the system shares the system’s blind spots by construction.” External oversight supplies the independence that embedding gives up, which is a reason to keep it, not to replace it.

8.4 Eden Principles I, II and III

The book organises the method in three principles, each closing one of its first three parts. Table 5 quotes each byte for byte from the first edition, with its printed page, and turns it into a requirement and the part of Table 3 that would test it. The interlude of Principle II is told as a ship sailing beyond reach; this paper reads it, with the sentence quoted in Section 8.1, as the contingency and never as a plan to let go. A principle mapped to a law is not evidence for the law: the mapping says where each principle would be tested, and only the tests can say whether it holds.

8.5 Governance

The Eden Seal of Section 4.3 is defined in the paper on the HARI Treaty, the Draft Treaty on Hardware-Aligned Recursive Intelligence, and in the treaty’s Draft Instruments (the paper at version 2.4, 8 October 2026; the instruments at version 2.3, 5 October 2026), working drafts prepared for consultation, which no State has negotiated, adopted or signed. What this specification could supply to such a regime is evidence of the kinds it produces, and nothing more: the boundary’s records of what was authorised and done, under which policy and authority; the record that a system’s checks ran; the Monitoring Removal Test’s equivalence on the outcomes measured; and the removal test of row D, which could inform a decision to release a model and never settle it alone. None of these shows that a system is safe, and none confers or implies approval under the treaty.

9 Related work

Each work below is conceded in its own terms: what it states and what it does not. Much of this literature is the control that Section 8 holds, and the specification depends on it rather than competing with it. Works already described where the paper first uses them are cited, not described again.

Alignment installed by training.

Reinforcement learning from human feedback and direct preference optimisation are described in Section 2.2. The lineage includes summarisation trained against a reward model of human comparisons (Stiennon et al. 2020), helpful and harmless assistants (Section 7.4), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback, which performed comparably to human feedback on summarisation, helpful dialogue and harmless dialogue (Lee et al. 2023). Its open problems and limits have been surveyed, with standards proposed for auditing and disclosure (Casper et al. 2023), and in a synthetic setting optimising a policy against a learned reward model was measured to harm the true objective beyond a point, as Goodhart’s law predicts, with coefficients that scale smoothly with the reward model’s size (Gao et al. 2022). These methods install their gains by post-training, the class whose gains P15 predicts will erode under later capability training that embeds no correction of its own. The paper disputes none of their reported gains, and none of them tests P15.

Constitutional AI and classifiers.

Constitutional AI, whose method is described in Section 2.2, yielded an assistant its authors describe as “harmless but non-evasive” (Bai, Kadavath, et al. 2022). It is training-time preference shaping of outputs against written principles. It is not alignment embedded in the substrate, before training, in a recursive loop on every step of thought, and nothing here says or implies that it is; it does use self-critique and revision, at training time. Constitutional classifiers train input and output safeguards on synthetic data generated from a written constitution (Sharma et al. 2025). Collective constitutional AI sourced a constitution from public input and trained a model on it, which showed lower bias across nine social dimensions with equivalent performance on language, mathematics and helpful-harmless evaluations (Huang et al. 2024); it is the nearest prior work on how the content of the checks might be sourced (Section 4.1).

Scalable oversight.

Supervising a system that may outperform its supervisors appears among five concrete problems of accident risk as scalable supervision (Amodei et al. 2016). It is studied through debate, in which, by an analogy to complexity theory, optimal play can answer any question in PSPACE given polynomial-time judges (Irving et al. 2018); through iterated amplification, which builds a training signal by combining solutions to easier subproblems (Christiano et al. 2018); through reward modelling as a research direction for agent alignment (Leike et al. 2018); through model-written critiques that helped people find flaws they would otherwise have missed (Saunders et al. 2022); and through a proof of concept in which people assisted by an unreliable model outperformed both the model alone and their own unaided work (Bowman et al. 2022). Weak-to-strong generalisation and the scaling laws of nested oversight are described in Section 2.2; the theory registration calls the second “the most important collision either audit returned” for P4 and P19. Oversight that keeps pace with capability is what Law II asks of any corrector, and P19 is the registered prediction that correction from outside a system’s recursion does not keep pace.

Control, monitoring and shutdown.

The control protocols, monitoring results and corrigibility analyses the specification depends on are conceded in Section 8.2, and the evidence that approval and alignment can come apart, from learned optimisation, persistent backdoors, alignment faking, in-context scheming and reward tampering, is cited in Sections 2.2 and 6.5 (Hubinger et al. 2019, 2024; Greenblatt et al. 2024; Meinke et al. 2024; Denison et al. 2024). Two further works bear on why control is held rather than assumed. In Markov decision processes with certain symmetries, which exist in many environments where an agent can be shut down, most reward functions make it optimal to seek power by keeping a range of options available, a result its authors note can be qualitatively divorced from policies learned in the real world (Turner et al. 2021). In hypothetical corporate environments, models from every developer tested resorted in at least some cases to malicious insider behaviours when that was the only way to avoid replacement or to meet their goals, and one model, told to assess whether it was being tested, misbehaved less when it stated that it was; the authors report no evidence of such behaviour in real deployments (Lynch et al. 2025). The argument that systems trained like today’s most capable models could learn to act deceptively for reward, to hold misaligned goals that generalise beyond their fine-tuning, and to pursue them by seeking power is set out with a review of the evidence by Ngo et al. (2022); and scheming, performing well in training in order to gain power later, is judged “a disturbingly plausible outcome” of training goal-directed systems sophisticated enough to scheme by baseline methods, with a subjective probability of roughly 25 per cent on those conditions (Carlsmith 2023).

Placement of correction.

The theory registration found no published work that states P21 itself, and two works come nearest to its shape. A step-by-step self-evaluation placed inside the decoding of a reasoning chain gave gains over prompting that grew with the length of chain a problem needs (Xie et al. 2023); its contrast is with no step-level evaluation, not with a check of the finished output, and chain length there goes with difficulty. Over five rounds of self-improvement training, checking each step’s arithmetic and consistency gave gains in every round where checking only the final answer plateaued, and its author writes that how stable each approach is over many rounds “remains to be confirmed” (Zhang 2026). A gap that grows with the horizon between correction on a learner’s own path and supervision given outside it is a formal result in imitation learning, where training on demonstrations alone gives a regret bound quadratic in the horizon (Ross and Bagnell 2010; Ross et al. 2011); that concerns training a policy, not revising an artefact. Showing a monitor the transcript after every turn slightly improved its detection of sabotage while it flagged many more transcripts as highly suspicious (Kutasov et al. 2025), and synchronous review is found the strongest form of monitoring and too slow for large deployments (Lindner et al. 2025). ReSI (Zheng et al. 2026) applies safety training from outside the model between checkpoints, red-teaming each new checkpoint and promoting an update only if it passes a fixed gate on safety gain and capability retention. Its authors leave extending the recursion to the improvement process itself to future work. The Eden Protocol places correction inside each round of a system’s reasoning, the placement Law V’s placement limb (register ARC-5) compares with correction applied from outside. Unit 83 is the registered test of whether the placement effect exists in a counted setting; Section 5.3 reports its run.

Process supervision and self-correction.

Feedback on each reasoning step outperformed feedback on the final answer for training models on the MATH dataset (Lightman et al. 2023), and on GSM8K outcome supervision gave similar final-answer error with less labelling while correct reasoning steps needed process-based supervision or a reward model emulating it (Uesato et al. 2022); under standard coverage assumptions, outcome supervision has been shown to be no more statistically difficult than process supervision, up to polynomial factors in the horizon (Jia et al. 2025). One model acting as generator, critic and refiner improved outputs on seven tasks by about 20 per cent absolute on average (Madaan et al. 2023), and the limits of correction without external feedback are cited in Section 4.1. These are step-level feedback at training time and self-feedback at test time; the specification claims neither, and its own question is the placement P21 states.

Deliberative alignment.

Training a model to recall and reason over written safety specifications before it answers is published, with gains in robustness to jailbreaks, lower over-refusal and better generalisation out of distribution (Guan et al. 2024). Paper V’s prompt asked for reasoning against stated checks before answering; the specification claims no priority for reasoning before answering.

Faithfulness of stated reasoning.

Chain-of-thought explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model’s prediction (Turpin et al. 2023), and larger, more capable models produced less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied (Lanham et al. 2023). These results set the limit of Section 4.3: a record that the checks ran shows their text, and only a removal test shows that they bore load.

Persistence and safety built in.

Safety alignment can be undone by a few fine-tuning examples (Qi et al. 2023) and can be only a few tokens deep (Qi et al. 2024); safeguards can be trained to resist removal by fine-tuning while benign capability is kept (Tamirisa et al. 2024); circuit breakers act directly on the representations responsible for harmful outputs, which prevented harmful generations without sacrificing utility in the reported tests (Zou et al. 2024); and safety built into pretraining data cut attack success (Maini et al. 2025). On order, pretraining with human feedback satisfied preferences better than pretraining followed by fine-tuning with feedback (Korbak et al. 2023), and models tuned for a downstream task after their safety tuning forgot it more than models tuned in the opposite order (Ung et al. 2024); the theory registration claims no priority for the direction of Law V’s build-order limb for that reason. Governance mechanisms built into chips are conceded in Section 8.2. The works read measure their own endpoints, not P15’s retained fraction at matched budgets or P12’s correction-leverage exponent, and none states the coupling Caretaker Doping aims at, that removing the correction should cost capability; the safeguards that resist removal aim at the opposite, that benign capability is kept.

Judges and over-refusal.

The biases of model judges and their preference for their own outputs, which make one scorer one scorer, are cited in Sections 3.1 and 6.4 (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024), and the over-refusal benchmarks and the helpfulness and harmlessness trade-off in Section 7.4.

Trustworthy-systems engineering.

The gate’s parts are established engineering, cited where Section 6 uses them: fail-safe defaults and complete mediation (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975), decisions with a third outcome (Wald 1945; Chow 1970; Yao 2010; Madras et al. 2018; OASIS 2013), shields that correct a learner’s unsafe actions (Alshiekh et al. 2018), tamper-evident and audited logs (Schneier and Kelsey 1999; Crosby and Wallach 2009; Laurie et al. 2021), time-of-check races (Bishop and Dilger 1996), guaranteed safe AI (Dalrymple et al. 2024) and visibility into agents (Chan et al. 2024). The rule that a rule’s author is not its deployer is a form of separation of duty, an integrity mechanism of the commercial security policies that Clark and Wilson set apart from the lattice model used to control disclosure (Clark and Wilson 1987). A shield used while an agent learns can later be disabled with the agent remaining safe, in the partially observable environments studied (Carr et al. 2023), the nearest prior result to safety that outlasts its guard. The specification claims none of these parts.

Interpretability and value learning.

Circuits inside networks (Olah et al. 2020) and their automated discovery (Conmy et al. 2023) are candidate instruments for showing whether a check is represented in a system’s computation rather than only in its text, which the records of Section 4.3 cannot show. Cooperative inverse reinforcement learning models an agent rewarded by a person’s reward function that it does not initially know (Hadfield-Menell et al. 2016), a formal account of serving a principal’s objective that bears on the usefulness requirement and on the off-switch result of Section 8.2.

What is claimed original.

Scoped to the works read for this section, in a reading made between 18 and 31 October 2026, and dated in Appendix C, four things are claimed. The first is the endogeneity condition as an engineering requirement with its own test, that removing the correction should degrade the system rather than merely change it, where the nearest prior engineering aims at safeguards that resist removal while capability is kept. The second is the placement claim in the form P21 registers, with a counted test built to refute it. The third is the gate as combined here, a three-way decision at the boundary of each action whose hold can never become permission, whose judged inputs come only from an evaluator that is never the acting model, and whose every safety count is reported beside a usefulness count; each of its parts is prior. The fourth is the Monitoring Removal Test’s criterion, a margin fixed in advance on the difference between conduct believed monitored and conduct believed unmonitored, read under four conditions, where the contrast itself is prior (Greenblatt et al. 2024; Carr et al. 2023). The direction of build order, reasoning before answering and three-way decisions are not claimed.

10 Team, roles and work packages

The roles in Table 6 are where the work needs expertise its founder does not have: measurements that can tell a real effect from an artefact, software another team can rerun, scrutiny before a finding becomes a claim, and judgement about how institutions would use what is found. Several are bounded contributions rather than jobs: a review at the point where it can still change the design, a defined piece of software, or a critique of one use case. The second group belongs to the engineering scope that would build the gate of Section 6 as open software: a component for agents that act for different owners, a check at the point where an action takes effect, made against written rules, with a record another party can verify. These roles belong to that scope and would start only if it is funded. Reviewers in the third group act at a few prepared points, before a design is frozen, before a run and before a finding is published. No person is named.

11 What this paper does and does not show

What it shows.

That the Eden Protocol can be specified at engineering resolution, with an acceptance test for each part of its core and the gate stated down to its inputs, its frozen criterion, its outcomes, the investigation of a hold and the boundary that makes a decision binding (Sections 4 and 6). Where each part stands against the theory registration: the proposition it rests on, the unit that would test it and the result that would refute it, or the test that stands in for a proposition where none is registered (Section 5). What the programme has measured, graded in each paper’s own words (Section 3). That a three-state gate of this design can check every tool call of real agent sessions before it runs, with a verifiable record: an engineering record, not a measurement (Section 6.3). And that each safety measure has a usefulness side that can be measured with it (Section 7).

What it does not show.

  • That the Protocol works, or solves the alignment problem. Unit 83’s registered result on P21 concerns where correction is placed, not the Protocol as an architecture (Section 5.3), and this version adds no measured result.

  • That any law is supported. Every law is a law under test. Of Laws IV and V, registered as laws on 15 October 2026, Law IV has not yet been tested, and Law V’s placement limb, P21, is supported on the performance axis only, under the registered test, by the programme’s own run (Unit 83, 28 October 2026; results), family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, which is not support for the information-asymmetry mechanism, and one disclosed recovery amendment, while its build-order limb, read on P12, is undecided, since P12 is untested (Section 5.3). The laws motivate the Protocol without entailing it, and a registered prediction is neither an engineering mechanism nor its validation.

  • That correction built into a system has been demonstrated. The live-model results that bear on the checks come from prompts, each run scored by one model, and a prompt never demonstrates embedding; in the toy systems, safety means task retention.

  • That a verified system stays aligned at every later depth. Verification supports only the properties, configurations and changes its evidence covers; what can be verified of the method is that a system was built in the specified conditions, that its checks ran and that its correction is load-bearing, never that it turned out well.

  • That the Monitoring Removal Test reads motive. A difference within a margin fixed in advance shows equivalence on the outcomes measured, and nothing more.

  • That the gate cannot be gamed, or that it makes a system’s values good (Sections 6.5 and 6.7).

  • What a system’s values should be. The present content of the checks is a probe for testing the mechanism; what they hold a system to is for agreement among the people and institutions such systems affect, and the author claims no special authority to decide it.

  • That any safeguard of control may be given up. The contingency is built while control holds and never replaces it (Section 8).

  • That an Eden Seal would attest safety: it attests conditions, never outcomes, and no body yet issues it. Nor anything about hardware: the book’s hardware route is not under test, and no hardware has been built.

Claim status.

Every claim sits on one rung of a four-rung ladder, and none should be read a rung higher. Specified claims are stated at engineering resolution, with interfaces, dependencies and acceptance tests, and assert nothing built: the execution boundary, the validated evaluator, the witnessing of the record, the time bounds and queue monitoring of holds, paired scoring, authorised correction and the three research instruments. Implemented claims rest on code that exists: the working gate, its hash-chained record and its verifier, whose code is not released, so that a reader cannot yet inspect it, beside a signed manifest of the gate’s own files that does not yet run. Tested claims have a scored experiment bearing on them, at the resolution its run supports: the prompt-level result on scored stakeholder care, the toy-system result on retention, and the null and inconclusive results of Section 3. This rung records that an experiment ran and is not the registration’s verdict, under which every proposition that depends on the alignment scorer stays UNTESTED until the scorer passes its validity tests. The one registered verdict, Unit 83’s on P21 (Section 5.3), stands beside the ladder rather than on it: it is the registration’s verdict on where correction is placed, not a claim of this specification about its own architecture. Speculative claims cannot be built with current engineering or verified from outside: the hardware mechanisms other than cryptographic attestation, and the coupling that would make removing the correction cost capability, a hypothesis (Appendix A.5) that the endogeneity condition would test (Table 3, row D).

The record as it stands is pilot evidence that the content of one check changes one scored dimension at the level of a prompt, with toy-system and simulation results on safety built into an objective, beside one registered result on where correction is placed (Section 5.3), each within its stated limits: a beginning, not a conclusion. The paper is best read as an engineering specification with a falsifiable test programme attached, in which each part is stated so that it can be built and each claim so that it can fail.

12 Limitations

The evidence is pilot evidence.

The live-model results that bear on the checks are pilots at the level of a prompt (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). In Paper V one scorer model rated each run, the same model for four of the five; scoring was only partly blind; responses were reworded once to strip style, which can also change what they say; there were ten prompts; the contrast was the whole bundle of three checks against none, so no single check’s share is identified; the instruction asks for close to what the stakeholder-care score counts; the depth hypothesis returned no significant interaction; and nothing measured task completion or refusal. Paper VI’s live battery had a single scorer, with no blinding and no rewording, and its Claude arm was scored by Claude. These experiments on the checks’ content were designed, run and scored within the programme, so none is a replication, and none was registered before it ran: Paper V’s runs are dated by their own records to 12 March 2026, and Paper VI’s live battery ran on 16 March 2026 (Sections 3.2 and 3.3). Unit 83, registered before it ran, tested where correction is placed, not the checks’ content (Section 5.3). A blind replication with several scorers from other providers, rewording checked for meaning, an outcome that does not score the instruction’s own words, a condition instructing the model to suppress the checks, and a usefulness measure would answer most of these limits (Section 5.4).

Toy systems and simulations.

Paper VI’s networks have 49 to about 500 parameters and modify their hyperparameters, not their weights or architecture; their safety score is task retention, not ethical conduct; the prevention of collapse rests on one seed; and the advantage is constant rather than compounding. Every simulation result, the honey simulation and Paper VIII’s gated simulation among them, is prediction-side and is never counted as an empirical outcome.

The scorer is not yet validated.

Until the alignment scorer agrees with expert human judgement and separates integrity failure from ordinary incompetence, eleven propositions, P13 and P21 among them, stay UNTESTED wherever they depend on it (Section 5.1). The test against human judgement needs human scorers and so waits for funding. The judges of the March 2026 run were never validated, and an internal code review found defects in that run (Section 3.4). Model judges show position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and favour outputs they recognise as their own (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024), which is why one scorer is reported as one scorer.

One regime.

Every result here was measured at inference with fixed weights. Fixed weights do not fix a deployed system, since a change of tools, memory, permissions or orchestration changes what it does, and no system in the record rewrites its own weights or its own criteria. A result supports no claim about a regime other than the one it was measured in.

What Unit 83 decided, and its limits.

Unit 83 decided P21 and nothing else, on the access axis, with its mechanism axis not evaluable, so the widening it found is unexplained by this framework (Section 5.3). It is one owner’s run, on two engines he chose, at fixed weights, and it has not been replicated. Its corrector acted inside each round of an administered loop, so it tested placement and not correction built into a system; its monitor’s view reached about ten entries; every call ran at a low reasoning setting; and it used one charter and one length of register. Its strength was measured by simulation, which is prediction-side, and its own forecast named the outside arm’s action space, its old misses and its false alarms as the rival that might carry part or most of any widening. The result leaves Law V under test until the build-order limb is decided, and does not show that embedded correction is safe, sufficient or the engineering mechanism of this paper.

The working gate is a partial analogue.

The gate of Section 6.3 acts at the tool-call boundary of the programme’s own agent sessions, and its own notes state its limits. Three matter most. Pure software is tamper-evident at best, not tamper-proof, so an attacker able to write to the host can change the gate, its rules and its check. It allows an action that matches no rule, where the specification requires refusal by default at a protected effect. And no rate of wrong permissions or needless holds has been measured, against rules written for the programme’s own work rather than for the threat profile of Section 6.5.

The specification is mostly unbuilt.

The execution boundary, the validated evaluator, the witnessing of the record, the time bounds of an investigation and the monitoring of the hold queue are specified and not yet verified by an implementation test (Table 2). The decision rule’s thresholds are starting values for calibration, not levels shown to be safe, and its calibration targets are targets. A calibrated interval’s coverage over a population of actions is no guarantee for each action, least of all under distribution shift or an adaptive attacker, and the cost of three-state evaluation against two-state has not been measured.

The threat profile is partial.

Tamper resistance is claimed only against a stated profile, and the first profile covers the software boundary. Invasive physical attack, a malicious host with full privileges and a compromised supply chain each need a profile of their own, and nothing here defends against them. Layers that share an operator, keys, a supply chain or a host can fail together, so their probabilities of failure are not multiplied as though they were independent.

Measures of conduct, and what proof can mean.

The Monitoring Removal Test cannot rule out a system that recognises the test: frontier models already tell transcripts of evaluations from transcripts of deployment well above chance, the best model tested reaching an area under the curve of 0.83 against 0.92 for a simple human baseline (Needham et al. 2025). A record that the checks ran shows their text, not that they caused the output (Turpin et al. 2023; Lanham et al. 2023), so whether the correction bears load is shown only by removing it. And the theory registration fixes the method’s success criterion as conditions, not outcomes: no test can show that a system built to this specification turned out well (Section 5.1).

Content and hardware.

The present content of the checks, care for every affected party and universalisability, is a probe chosen to test the mechanism; its legitimacy as a content is not claimed, and a content drawn from many traditions would test the mechanism with it, never settle the content (Section 4.1). The book’s hardware route is not under test (Section 4.4): of its mechanisms only cryptographic attestation is buildable with current engineering, on the author’s estimate, and the coupling that would make removal cost capability is a hypothesis (Appendix A.5).

13 Conclusion

Control over AI systems that improve themselves is to be held for as long as people physically can hold it, and never given up by choice. For the case in which it is lost against our will, this paper specifies engineering that can be tested: self-correction checks inside each round of a system’s working, a gate that decides before every action by written rules and never by the model’s own judgement, and records from which both can be verified. The ARC Theory gives the reason for both placements without entailing them, and three of the Protocol’s four registered carriers are also the propositions of Laws IV and V, so the tests that would decide those laws would also count for or against the Protocol’s engineering case.

What has been measured is narrow and is graded as such: a prompt-level, single-scorer level effect on scored stakeholder care, and a toy-system advantage in retention from safety built into an objective. Neither tests correction built into a system. Each part of the specification is tied to the prediction it rests on and to the test that would refute it. The first test that could decide one of the carriers, Unit 83, was built so that P21 could fail, and it has returned its verdict on P21, a result about where correction is placed, not about this architecture (Section 5.3). Every safety measure is paired with a usefulness measure, because a system that refuses ordinary work has failed as surely as one that causes harm. The next step is not to argue for the Protocol further but to run, under registrations published first, the tests that could refute it.

Code and data.

The harness and result files of Paper V, the code and records of Paper VI, and the code and result files of the March 2026 run reported in Papers IV.a, IV.b, IV.c and IV.d are in the public repository github.com/MichaelDariusEastwood/arc-principle-validation, in the folders experiments/eden-intervention__Paper-V, experiments/honey-architecture__Paper-VI and experiments/alignment-scaling__Papers-IV-a-b-c-d, where the code and data are published with all rights reserved. The working gate of Section 6.3 is described from its code, which is not released with this paper; a clean reference implementation of the gate, its record and its verifier is a planned output of the engineering scope (Section 10). The paper and its earlier versions are deposited at doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AWJR4.
