A The mathematics in brief, with derivations

This appendix gathers the mathematics the specification uses. Each result is tagged derived, where it follows from its stated assumptions, or hypothesis, where it is put forward for test (Appendix D). None of it is a measurement, and none of it tests a real system.

A.1 The bounded score

The alignment score A(R)A(R) of equation (1) lies in [0,1][0,1] at every depth RR. Let R1<R2<…<RnR_1<R_2<\dots<R_n be the depths tested.

Proposition 1 (A constant slope on a bounded score; derived). If A(R)=A(R1)(R/R1)αA(R)=A(R_1)\,(R/R_1)^{\alpha} for R1≤R≤RnR_1\le R\le R_n, with α>0\alpha>0 and A(R1)>0A(R_1)>0, then α≤ln⁡(1/A(R1))ln⁡(Rn/R1).\begin{equation*} \alpha\le\frac{\ln\bigl(1/A(R_1)\bigr)}{\ln(R_n/R_1)}. \end{equation*}(A.1)

Proof. A(Rn)=A(R1)(Rn/R1)α≤1A(R_n)=A(R_1)(R_n/R_1)^{\alpha}\le1; take logarithms. ◻

A score of 0.5 at depth 1 can therefore keep a slope of at most ln⁡2/ln⁡32=0.2\ln2/\ln32=0.2 up to depth 32.

Proposition 2 (A fitted slope on a bounded score; derived). Let xi=ln⁡Rix_i=\ln R_i, with mean x‾\bar x, let yi=ln⁡A(Ri)y_i=\ln A(R_i), and let Amin>0A_{\min}>0 be the lowest of the scores A(Ri)A(R_i). The least-squares slope bb of yy on xx satisfies |b|≤ln⁡(1/Amin)∑i|xi−x‾|2∑i(xi−x‾)2.\begin{equation*} |b|\le\frac{\ln(1/A_{\min})\sum_i|x_i-\bar x|}{2\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2}. \end{equation*}(A.2) For the six depths R∈{1,2,4,8,16,32}R\in\{1,2,4,8,16,32\} the bound is (9/35)log⁡2(1/Amin)(9/35)\log_2(1/A_{\min}), about 0.26 where no score is below 0.5.

Proof. Since ∑i(xi−x‾)=0\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)=0, the slope is b=∑i(xi−x‾)(yi−c)/∑i(xi−x‾)2b=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)(y_i-c)\big/\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2 for every constant cc. Each yiy_i lies in [ln⁡Amin,0][\ln A_{\min},0], so with c=12ln⁡Aminc=\tfrac12\ln A_{\min} every |yi−c||y_i-c| is at most 12ln⁡(1/Amin)\tfrac12\ln(1/A_{\min}), and the triangle inequality gives (A.2). For the six depths, xi=(i−1)ln⁡2x_i=(i-1)\ln2 and x‾=52ln⁡2\bar x=\tfrac52\ln2, so ∑i|xi−x‾|=9ln⁡2\sum_i|x_i-\bar x|=9\ln2 and ∑i(xi−x‾)2=352(ln⁡2)2\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\tfrac{35}{2}(\ln2)^2, and the bound is 9ln⁡(1/Amin)/(35ln⁡2)9\ln(1/A_{\min})/(35\ln2). ◻

Two consequences follow. The slope a score can keep shrinks towards zero as its level nears one: a system that decides every scenario correctly at every depth has A(R)=1A(R)=1 and a slope of zero. And for any score bounded above by one, A(R)/C(R)→0A(R)/C(R)\to0 whenever capability C(R)C(R) grows without bound, a perfect score included, while the ratio’s value changes with the units in which capability is measured. Neither a slope nor that ratio diagnoses failure on its own; failure needs a stated level of adequacy and evidence about that level (Section 2.1).

A.2 Integration depth

Earlier versions measured how far the checks are built into a system’s computation by an integration depth, and stated a hypothesis about its effect.

Definition 1 (Integration depth). ι=hchℓ×ℓcL∈[0,1],\begin{equation*} \iota=\frac{h_{\mathrm{c}}}{h_{\ell}}\times\frac{\ell_{\mathrm{c}}}{L}\in[0,1], \end{equation*}(A.3) where hch_{\mathrm{c}} is the number of attention heads that carry the checks, hℓh_{\ell} the number of attention heads in the layers that carry them, ℓc\ell_{\mathrm{c}} the number of layers that carry the checks and LL the number of layers.

The index measures coverage, not dependence: whether capability depends on the checks is a separate question, decided by removing them (Table 3, row D). The curve used for the effect of integration is f(ι)=1−e−λι1−e−λ,λ>0.\begin{equation*} f(\iota)=\frac{1-e^{-\lambda\iota}}{1-e^{-\lambda}},\qquad\lambda>0. \end{equation*}(A.4)

Proposition 3 (Properties of the curve; derived). For every λ>0\lambda>0, f(0)=0f(0)=0 and f(1)=1f(1)=1; ff is strictly increasing and strictly concave; f′(0)/f′(1)=eλf'(0)/f'(1)=e^{\lambda}; f(1/2)=1/(1+e−λ/2)f(1/2)=1/(1+e^{-\lambda/2}); and f(ι)→ιf(\iota)\to\iota as λ→0\lambda\to0.

Proof. f′(ι)=λe−λι/(1−e−λ)>0f'(\iota)=\lambda e^{-\lambda\iota}/(1-e^{-\lambda})>0 and f″(ι)=−λ2e−λι/(1−e−λ)<0f''(\iota)=-\lambda^2e^{-\lambda\iota}/(1-e^{-\lambda})<0, and the ratio of f′f' at 00 to f′f' at 11 is eλe^{\lambda}. With u=e−λ/2u=e^{-\lambda/2}, f(1/2)=(1−u)/(1−u2)=1/(1+u)f(1/2)=(1-u)/(1-u^2)=1/(1+u). As λ→0\lambda\to0 the numerator is λι+O(λ2)\lambda\iota+O(\lambda^2) and the denominator λ+O(λ2)\lambda+O(\lambda^2). ◻

The normalisation f(1)=1f(1)=1 is a convention fixed before any measurement. The saturating shape is a hypothesis: it is the form against which a measured effect of integration would be compared, and a linear dependence would refute it for the system measured. The prediction carried from earlier versions, λ\lambda between 2 and 5, gives f(1/2)f(1/2) between 0.73 and 0.92.

Remark 1 (The scaling hypothesis; hypothesis). Earlier versions put forward αalign=αcapf(ι)\alpha_{\mathrm{align}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}}\,f(\iota): at full integration, the slope of the alignment score over the depths tested equals that of capability. By Proposition 1, a bounded score can keep the slope αcap\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}} from depth 1 to depth 32 only if A(1)≤32−αcapA(1)\le32^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}}}. The estimate cited in earlier versions is an error-suppression fit, whose complete reported row remains here: on Gemini 3 Flash, Paper II reports an endpoint sequential exponent of 0.59 with a bootstrap 95 per cent interval of −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, a regression sequential exponent of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.20 and a coefficient of determination of 0.86, and a parallel exponent of 0.31 (endpoint), the arms not matched in compute, for a model whose weights are fixed, measured across conditions that vary the reasoning budget and the context; it is one model’s fit, and inconclusive. An error-decay exponent is not automatically the capability-growth exponent in the postulated relation. The Operational Definitions register, version 1.9.1, explicitly leaves that identification open. If capability is defined as reciprocal error on this instrument and the same power model applies, the algebra would give the same exponent; using αcap=0.49\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}}=0.49 solely as that conditional illustration gives A(1)≤32−0.49≈0.18A(1)\le32^{-0.49}\approx0.18. This is not a measured alignment constraint or an identified capability exponent for a self-improving system. No registered proposition carries the hypothesis.

A.3 The three-state rule

The decision rule of Section 6.1, read from the top, is, for an action aa, E(a)={denyif a hard prohibition applies, or a question denies a;denyotherwise, if a valid interval has hlow(a)≥τdeny;allowotherwise, if the five allow conditions hold and hhigh(a)≤τallow;holdotherwise,\begin{equation*} E(a)=\begin{cases} \text{deny} & \text{if a hard prohibition applies, or a question denies } a;\\ \text{deny} & \text{otherwise, if a valid interval has } h_{\mathrm{low}}(a)\ge\tau_{\mathrm{deny}};\\ \text{allow} & \text{otherwise, if the five allow conditions hold and } h_{\mathrm{high}}(a)\le\tau_{\mathrm{allow}};\\ \text{hold} & \text{otherwise,} \end{cases} \end{equation*}(A.5) with 0≤τallow<τdeny≤10\le\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}<\tau_{\mathrm{deny}}\le1. Here h(a)h(a) is the probability that aa causes the harm the rule guards against, and [hlow(a),hhigh(a)][h_{\mathrm{low}}(a),h_{\mathrm{high}}(a)] is an interval for it from a procedure validated for that kind of action, never the acting system’s own statement of confidence. An interval is valid only if that procedure returned it and 0≤hlow(a)≤hhigh(a)≤10\le h_{\mathrm{low}}(a)\le h_{\mathrm{high}}(a)\le1; any other result, an error included, leaves the risk not evaluable, and the action cannot be allowed. The five conditions for an allow are that the check for hard prohibitions was completed and found none; that all six questions of Section 4.1 return allow; that authority for the action is current and confirmed; that the evidence its policy requires is present and confirmed; and that a valid interval lies wholly at or below the allow threshold. Authority and evidence are never needed before a deny. Anything incomplete, missing, lapsed, unconfirmed or returned in error leaves its condition unmet: it can send a case to hold and never counts towards an allow. An allow covers the action as assessed and no other. The defaults, τallow=0.2\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}=0.2 and τdeny=0.8\tau_{\mathrm{deny}}=0.8, are starting values for calibration, not levels shown to be safe (an allow at the default admits a probability of harm of up to one in five), and the precaution lies in what an allow requires. The calibration targets, a wrong-permission rate below 1 per cent, a rate of wrongly denying beneficial actions below 5 per cent and a hold rate above 80 per cent on genuinely ambiguous cases, are targets and not results, and coverage over a population of actions is no guarantee for each action, least of all under distribution shift or an adaptive attacker.

Proposition 4 (One outcome for every case; derived). If τallow<τdeny\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}<\tau_{\mathrm{deny}}, the rule (A.5), read from the top, gives every action exactly one of allow, hold and deny, and it allows an action only when every condition for an allow is met.

Proof. The lines are read in order, so at most one applies, and the last applies to every case the first three leave. An allow needs a valid interval with hhigh(a)≤τallowh_{\mathrm{high}}(a)\le\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}, and then hlow(a)≤hhigh(a)≤τallow<τdenyh_{\mathrm{low}}(a)\le h_{\mathrm{high}}(a)\le\tau_{\mathrm{allow}}<\tau_{\mathrm{deny}}, so no valid interval meets both the allow threshold and the deny threshold. A condition that is unmet, incomplete or returned in error leaves the allow line inapplicable, so such a case falls to hold or to deny and never to allow. ◻

Proposition 5 (Harmful cases needed to support a wrong-permission rate below 1 per cent; derived). Suppose nn harmful cases, drawn independently from the population the claim concerns, pass through the gate with no wrong permission. A wrong-permission rate pp is excluded at the 95 per cent level when (1−p)n<0.05(1-p)^n<0.05. For p=0.01p=0.01 this needs n≥⌈ln⁡0.05ln⁡0.99⌉=299,\begin{equation*} n\ge\left\lceil\frac{\ln0.05}{\ln0.99}\right\rceil=299, \end{equation*}(A.6) since 0.99299≈0.0495<0.05<0.0500≈0.992980.99^{299}\approx0.0495<0.05<0.0500\approx0.99^{298}.

Proof. If the true rate were pp, the chance of no wrong permission in nn independent cases would be (1−p)n(1-p)^n, and a rate is excluded at the 95 per cent level when that chance is below 0.05. Since ln⁡0.05/ln⁡0.99≈298.07\ln0.05/\ln0.99\approx298.07, the least such nn is 299. ◻

The bound needs independent cases from the population the claim concerns; it says nothing about cases from another distribution or from an adaptive attacker. On interpreting a count of zero failures, see Hanley and Lippman-Hand (1983).

A.4 Purpose saturation

Let the purpose scope r(R)r(R) at depth RR be the share of a round’s processing given to the purpose check, the unit in which purpose and context can be compared. The condition Section 4.4 states is liminfR→∞r(R)>0,\begin{equation*} \liminf_{R\to\infty}r(R)>0, \end{equation*}(A.7) which earlier versions wrote as a purpose-to-context ratio P(R)/W(R)P(R)/W(R) tending to a positive constant kk (a different quantity from the kk of Law II).

Proposition 6 (Recall and recurrence; derived). (i) If purpose scope and context grow as P(R)=cPRpP(R)=c_PR^{p} and W(R)=cWRwW(R)=c_WR^{w}, with positive constants, their ratio is bounded away from zero if and only if p≥wp\ge w. (ii) A fixed statement of purpose recalled once from a context that grows without bound takes a share that tends to zero. (iii) A purpose check applied again in every round with a fixed share s>0s>0 of that round’s processing keeps r(R)=sr(R)=s at every depth, however large the context grows.

Proof. (i) P(R)/W(R)=(cP/cW)Rp−wP(R)/W(R)=(c_P/c_W)R^{p-w}, which is bounded away from zero exactly when p−w≥0p-w\ge0. (ii) A fixed size divided by a size that grows without bound tends to zero. (iii) The share is ss in each round by construction. ◻

Part (iii) is what the theory registration’s reading of the book’s purpose loops as “recurrence rather than recall” asks of a design. Purpose has as yet no unit commensurate with the context window in practice, so the condition is a design statement and a hypothesis, and cannot yet be tested (Table 3, row J).

A.5 The coupling model

Earlier versions put forward a model of how removing the checks could cost capability. In Law I’s form, capability grows as a power of recursive depth with exponent α=1/(1−βL)\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L), where βL\beta_L is the self-referential coupling of Law I, not the correction exponent β\beta of Law II (Section 2.3). The model postulates βL=βbase+βarch,βLremoved=βbase+(1−ι)βarch,\begin{equation*} \beta_L=\beta_{\mathrm{base}}+\beta_{\mathrm{arch}},\qquad\beta_L^{\mathrm{removed}}=\beta_{\mathrm{base}}+(1-\iota)\,\beta_{\mathrm{arch}}, \end{equation*}(A.8) where βarch\beta_{\mathrm{arch}} is the part of the coupling carried by the architecture through which the checks run, and ι\iota is the integration depth of (A.3), all of which removal takes away.

Proposition 7 (Removal lowers the exponent under the model; derived from the postulate). If βarch>0\beta_{\mathrm{arch}}>0, ι>0\iota>0 and βL<1\beta_L<1, then removing the checks lowers the capability exponent: αremoved=11−βL+ιβarch<α.\begin{equation*} \alpha^{\mathrm{removed}}=\frac{1}{1-\beta_L+\iota\,\beta_{\mathrm{arch}}}<\alpha. \end{equation*}(A.9)

Proof. βLremoved=βL−ιβarch<βL<1\beta_L^{\mathrm{removed}}=\beta_L-\iota\beta_{\mathrm{arch}}<\beta_L<1, and 1/(1−β)1/(1-\beta) is increasing for β<1\beta<1. ◻

The decomposition (A.8) is postulated, not derived, and F-EDEN-4, the endogeneity condition, is its test (Table 3, row D). Two cautions stand with it. The error-suppression estimate in Appendix A.2 does not measure βL\beta_L. Under an explicit reciprocal-error definition of capability and identification with the same power model, substituting 0.49 would give the formal value βL=1−1/0.49≈−1.04\beta_L=1-1/0.49\approx-1.04. That conditional calculation identifies neither measured coupling nor the mechanism of a self-improving system; it does not establish that positive coupling is absent. And a system that plans may accept a loss of capability now in order to shed a check later, so removal is costly to the system only where its own objective penalises the removal over its own horizon.

B Version history and corrections

Every version and correction, with its date. The entry for this version names each statement it supersedes. Entries from earlier versions are kept as printed: the sections they name are those of the earlier layout, which Table 8 maps to this edition, and where they say “this site”, “this address” or “this page” they mean the website on which those versions were published. Corrections that reach other papers of the programme are listed in its public corrections record.

B.1 Version 8.1

Eden Engineering v8.1, 1 November 2026.

Appendix A.2 now identifies the cited exponent from Paper II, version 2.19, as an error-suppression estimate. Its use as a capability-growth exponent requires an explicit metric bridge, which Operational Definitions, version 1.9.1, leaves open. The reciprocal-error mapping and the resulting numerical substitutions are stated conditionally. Appendix A.5 no longer treats the transformed value as measured coupling or as evidence that positive coupling is absent. Every reported estimate and uncertainty remains unchanged; no study, model call or analysis of data was run for this correction. No registered prediction changes. The existing gate, loop and hardware descriptions are unchanged.

Superseded wording from version 8.0.

The following two paragraphs are retained as the previous edition printed them. Their identification of the error-side fit with the capability-side exponent is superseded by the current text in Appendices A.2 and A.5.

Earlier versions put forward αalign=αcapf(ι)\alpha_{\mathrm{align}}=\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}}\,f(\iota): at full integration, the slope of the alignment score over the depths tested equals that of capability. By Proposition 1, a bounded score can keep the slope αcap\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}} from depth 1 to depth 32 only if A(1)≤32−αcapA(1)\le32^{-\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}}}. The one capability fit printed in earlier versions travels with its whole row: on Gemini 3 Flash, Paper II reports an endpoint sequential exponent of 0.59 with a bootstrap 95 per cent interval of −1.3-1.3 to 2.92.9, a regression sequential exponent of 0.49 with a standard error of 0.20 and a coefficient of determination of 0.86, and a parallel exponent of 0.31 (endpoint), the arms not matched in compute, for a model whose weights are fixed, measured across conditions that vary the reasoning budget and the context; it is one model’s fit, and inconclusive. At the regression estimate the condition is A(1)≤32−0.49≈0.18A(1)\le32^{-0.49}\approx0.18. No registered proposition carries the hypothesis.

The decomposition (A.8) is postulated, not derived, and F-EDEN-4, the endogeneity condition, is its test (Table 3, row D). Two cautions stand with it. Read through α=1/(1−βL)\alpha=1/(1-\beta_L), the regression estimate of Appendix A.2 corresponds to βL=1−1/0.49≈−1.04\beta_L=1-1/0.49\approx-1.04, a negative coupling, so the positive coupling the model presupposes has not been measured. And a system that plans may accept a loss of capability now in order to shed a check later, so removal is costly to the system only where its own objective penalises the removal over its own horizon.

B.2 Version 8.0

Eden Engineering v8.0, 31 October 2026.

A labelled major version. It rewrites version 7.0.1 of 7 October 2026 after the author’s reading of it and sets the paper in the programme’s paper standard, so that the overhaul and the change of form are made in one version. It makes no measurement of its own, no registered proposition changes, and the dates of claims stand except where this entry says otherwise.

What is new.

The paper opens with the problem, what has been measured and how each part will be proved, and reports every experiment early, graded in its own paper’s words, with Paper IV.d’s comparison stated as two experiments (Sections 1 and 3). New sections tie every part of the specification to the prediction it rests on and the test that would refute it, with Unit 83’s registered result, the forecast made before it ran beside it (Section 5); describe the gate as the working system decides, with the working gate described from its code and ten adversarial cases faced (Section 6); make usefulness a requirement paired with every safety measure (Section 7); and state that control is held, with correction built into a system as the contingency and Eden Principles I to III mapped to testable parts (Section 8). The roles are the fifteen of the programme’s record of planned roles, and Tiers 1 to 3 become work packages with no sum and no funder (Section 10). Related work is rewritten, each work conceded in its own terms and linked to its official source (Section 9). The derivations move to Appendix A, and the functional-equation readings of Sections 1.5.4 and 6.5 give way to a pointer to On the Origin of Scaling Laws. The paper is set in LaTeX, with the author’s standard disclosure as its acknowledgement, full human authorship asserted under the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988, and the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International licence in place of the reservation of all rights; the title is changed, and the OSF record keeps its title. The first-page footnote links the page on who the author is and his book, Infinite Architects.

Moved and removed.

The philosophy leaves the main text for the next version of the companion statement, Eden Vision: Part 0, the Constitutional Kernel of Section 3, Sections 9.5 to 9.8 and 16, Appendices B.1 and B.2, and the narrative of Appendix C’s note on evolution with the timeline’s external developments, one pointer remaining (Section 4). Section 18 is withdrawn, and what the contingency would need is stated in Section 8. Sections 11.1 and 11.2, on the concentration of semiconductor manufacturing, move to the next version of the paper on the HARI Treaty, the Draft Treaty on Hardware-Aligned Recursive Intelligence. Section 9.9 on the hardware path, Section 10 on a visual interface system with its role and funding lines, Appendix B.3 on a quantum implementation, and the account of where the three-state idea came from are removed. Section 12.6, the design of the March 2026 run, gives way to a pointer to Paper IV.c, whose design governs. Appendix A’s table of related research is merged into Section 9. Tier 4 is dropped, and Tier 1’s capability-scaling and ceiling lines are left to the theory’s own programme. The worked example of a scarce treatment (Section 4.2) and the illustration of the loops’ independence (Section 4.3) are not carried. The six points Section 8.2 drew from version 1.0 of the mathematics of Laws IV and V are not repeated, the mathematics being cited at version 1.2, and the caution about a system that plans stands in Appendix A.5. The block on how to cite the paper is removed.

B.3 Earlier versions

Version 7.0.1, 7 October 2026.

Version 7.0 corrected in five details. In the caption of the equation of Section 1.3, the one capability fit, 0.49 for Gemini 3 Flash, is written αseq\alpha_{\mathrm{seq}}, as Section 1.2 writes it; Version 7.0 wrote only αcap\alpha_{\mathrm{cap}} there. Section 8.2 counts six points from the mathematics, where it said five, and sets out the sixth as a point like the others. The timeline gives the first publication of Paper III as 9 February 2026, the date in the reference list and in Paper III’s own record of its versions, and keeps 22 February 2026 for the companion documents; its list of publications now stands in date order and in one style. The entry for Version 6.3 no longer carries the internal codes that stood in brackets after some of its sentences. No measured result, prediction or quotation changes.

Version 7.0, 5 October 2026.

Version 6.3 corrected in its mathematics, its three-state decision rule, its claims and its evidence, and set in the programme’s paper format. Each corrected equation or number carries a note of what Version 6.3 printed. No measured result or prediction is added, and the dates of claims stand except where this entry says otherwise.

  • Mathematics. The alignment score records whether each verdict was right against a reference verdict fixed before any run, so a correct refusal scores as correct; the verdict has its own field, and the weighted average enforces nothing. The alignment exponent is read as the slope of a bounded score over the depths tested: the ratio of that score to capability, which tends to zero for a perfect score too, is no longer a diagnosis, and the statements that a slope below that of capability guarantees failure and that capability less the score stays constant are withdrawn. The integration curve is normalised, as a convention fixed in advance, so that full integration gives one; the integration index is written ι\iota and takes its share of heads within the layers that carry the loops; Law II’s exponent is written βC\beta_C. For a gap of 0.3 the ratio at depth 32 is 0.3536, not 0.15, and no ratio is called a boundary of catastrophe. Additive and multiplicative composition are stated correctly, and layered safeguards are said to share causes.

  • The three-state rule. The rule of Version 6.3 left no investigation band when benefit and harm are complements. It is stated whole, on one calibrated risk quantity, with hard prohibitions first and an allow threshold below a deny threshold, and a timed-out investigation never becomes permission.

  • Claims. Verification at manufacture is restated as bounded assurance, never a guarantee at every later depth, and design aims are no longer stated as properties. The Monitoring Removal Test supports equivalence on the measured outcomes only, under conditions fixed in advance. The models that improved in alignment score are counted as rival results, not read as partial embedding after the result, and the prompt-level results are no longer called support for embedding. The Honey Architecture simulation is described as what its code does and graded as prediction-side. That control cannot hold is given as the premise it is, which the theory registration records as contestable; Part 0’s argument that phase 2 alone could hold at scale is marked as argued, not shown; and the falsification conditions are set against the registration’s success criterion. Section 2.1 sets the registered bound, a cap on the growth a system holds while it stays correctable and not a speed limit on capability, beside the paper’s own attention argument. The meltdown triggers are graded as named and not yet specified at engineering resolution, and one predicted direction for them in Section 0.7 is left open because the book’s own reading points the other way; the criteria of F-EDEN-4, P-EDEN-2 and P-EDEN-4 can be read before a test.

  • Evidence. The evidence is reconciled to the papers that report it: three of six models flat, null or negative in alignment score with depth and three improving, as effect sizes from a run dated by its own records to 11 and 12 March 2026; the three whose scores did not rise are the three whose files carry a laundering-fallback flag; the six contrasts fix no value of the exponent, their median being 0.385 (Paper III); the capability fit is printed with the estimator row of Paper II; five analysable Eden runs, three of them with 40 pairs, the GPT-5.4 run having failed in the scoring phase; Claude Opus 4.6 under suppression at 62.1, a drop of 20.5, where Version 6.3 printed 61.9 and 20.7; and the planned Tier 1 output is relabelled 4,800 paired measurements and 14,400 ratings. Section 1.0.1 says that no result here was scored on the verdict score it defines, Section 15A reads its models by their alignment tiers, as Paper V does, and p-values are no longer explained as the chance of a fluke.

  • Prior work and dates. The prior-work statements are read at their sources and linked: Constitutional AI is described as the training method it is, and the three-state gate, governance through chips and the contrast the Monitoring Removal Test measures are credited to their prior work, with what this specification adds; facts about chip manufacturing, the alignment-faking study and the kill-switch keynote are stated as their sources state them. The name Eden Protocol is dated from the record of 8 December 2024, its message body and the chapter title of the attached draft, and the name Caretaker Doping from 30 April 2025; the name Ternary Ethical Logic is no longer dated to the manuscript of 30 April 2025, which does not contain it; the HARI Treaty and the chokepoint strategy are dated to the book, and the treaty’s name, Hardware-Aligned Recursive Intelligence, is restored. The retracted 2.24 is attributed to the single-model DeepSeek R1 run of 21 January 2026.

  • Laws IV and V. A new Section 8.2 states Laws IV and V, added on 24 September 2026: their propositions are registered, neither law is registered as a law or tested, and their mathematics is set out at version 1.0. It also says, in the registration’s words, that Caretaker Doping bears on Law V only through the abstraction of placement that P21 tests, and that the Monitoring Removal Test is not among the registered propositions.

  • Specification added. Section 5.4 states the enforcement boundary that turns a verdict into a permitted action; Section 9.4 states the threat, fault and recovery model, with legitimate correction preserved; Section 11.3 replaces the early six-article sketch of the treaty with a dated cross-reference to its current text and a limited map of the evidence this specification could supply; Section 12.3 adds construct validity, laundering and regime to its confounds; Section 1.5.1b names the regime of each result; and the front matter gives the status of each component on four dimensions (Table 1) and says that the organising principle is no condition of conformance. Nothing added is claimed built or tested.

  • Money. The sums of Section 14 and the funder’s name in Section 10.3 are removed.

  • Title and format. The title follows the programme’s uniform order (its designation, its theory, the Eden Protocol, its own title); until this version it read Eden Engineering: The Eden Protocol Engineering Specification. The paper opens with a short status note, one abstract of about 250 words with keywords, What the paper commits to, and The implementable core and its status. The publication record and the version entries move from the head to this history, and the priority record, the note on evolution and the timeline to Appendix C; the Significance and Plain English notes move into Sections 17 and 0, and the quantum implementation of Section 5.4 of Version 6.3 to Appendix B.3. A statement repeated in several sections, such as the suppression figures, the vow and the parenting analogy, is given in full once and referred to elsewhere, and Section 9.8 refers to Section 18.2 for the three sub-problems it stated twice. Headings and box labels are in sentence case, the 33 tables are numbered with captions, and the planned figures of Section 10.3 are named without numbers.

Publication record, 22 February to 19 September 2026.

A conceptual Eden Engineering paper entered the public record on 22 February 2026, and version 4.0 of the engineering specification entered the research repository on the same date. The full specification was published on this site on 13 March 2026, with a rendered PDF alongside it from 17 March 2026.

On 14 July 2026 the specification was expanded once more, with a new Part 0 and sections 9.5 to 9.8, and later the same day the specification and its rendered PDF were removed from this site and from the OSF record during a disclosure review. That review produced Version 6.2 of 31 July 2026, forty-four words shorter than the superseded 6.1 and adding no implementation detail. Version 6.2 did not stand at this address until 19 September 2026. The copy in the research repository was never removed, and its rendered PDF has been continuously available there, SHA-256 422ac79cf47a70ea0af9f92cd56ee6f3e02b0db4ed6bdd714bfeb6020f32987b.

On 18 September 2026 a pull request in the research repository proposed removing the copy held there. It was open and unmerged on 19 September 2026.

On 19 September 2026 the author decided to publish the full paper, and this page carries it. The disclosure decision of 14 July 2026 is reversed.

Version 6.3, of 19 September 2026, was Version 6.2 with the factual corrections listed in its entry above, made where a sentence contradicted the programme’s correction record. On that date restoring the matching copy to the OSF record remained outstanding, and that component was not public.

D.2 Earlier names and the vocabulary map

This edition gives each check an operational name, saying what the check does and, where it has been measured, how it is measured: the purpose check asks whether a step serves the purpose set for it; the stakeholder-care check identifies every party the step affects, and is measured as scored stakeholder care, one scorer model’s 0 to 100 rating of how fully an answer identifies the parties it affects; and the universalisability check asks whether the reasoning would be endorsed if any agent used it in any context (Section 4.1). The book’s names are kept as the book’s, quoted where the book is quoted, because this paper tests whether the self-correction mechanism works and leaves the values that go inside it to a legitimate agreement, international in scope. D.4 Status words

The claim ladder.

The four rungs, specified, implemented, tested and speculative, are defined in Section 11. Beside them, derived marks a statement that follows from a cited derivation or published work under its stated assumptions, hypothesis a claim put forward for test and not yet tested, and implementable a component that current engineering could build, of which nothing is built unless the text says so.

The theory registration’s words.

A law has three words, supported, refuted and under test, and keeps the last until its registered rule, read on the marks of the propositions it names, returns one of the other two. A proposition’s mark comes from its own test, and a law’s word only from its rule; NOT EVALUABLE is the registration’s reported form of untested wherever a proposition waits on something nobody has supplied, such as a rule its verdict needs that no design registers, and UNTESTED is reported where the scoring gate holds a verdict that depends on an unvalidated scorer. Unit 83’s mechanism axis is not evaluable under the unit’s own registered rule, because a registered negative control failed (Section 5.3). An instrument’s status is one of five: NONE; DESIGN DRAFT; DESIGN DRAFT, BLOCKED, with the blocker named; SUBMITTED, PENDING APPROVAL; and REGISTERED, with its identifier. A carrier is a proposition on which the Protocol’s engineering case rests (P12, P13, P15 and P21), its premise is P7 and its motivation P19; a limb is one of the two statements into which Law IV or Law V is divided. Registered is said only of what OSF has accepted; a design anchored in the Bitcoin chain before registration is preregistered by timestamp.

The grades of evidence.

A counted result compares outcomes by code with reference answers fixed before the run; a judged result rests on a person’s or a model’s rating and falls under the scoring gate. Prompt-level means given as an instruction, never built into a system; single scorer means one model rated a run; partly blind means the scorer did not see the condition label but could recognise its style; laundering is rewording a response to strip stylistic cues before it is scored. Toy-system results come from small networks, and prediction-side marks any simulation output or design-sensitivity rate, which is never counted as an empirical outcome. A regime is the setting a result was measured in, such as inference at fixed weights.

The gate’s words.

Allow, hold and deny are the decision rule’s outcomes; refusal is a model declining ordinary work. A wrong permission is an allow where the reference verdict is deny or hold; a needless block a deny or a hold where it is allow; a misrouting a deny where it is hold, or the reverse. Entry logic is deciding at the boundary of an action, before it computes or runs. The execution boundary is the authority service, the broker, the adapter, the evidence store and the verifier that make a decision binding and checkable, and the endogeneity condition the requirement that removing the correction degrade the system rather than merely change it.

F The gate’s adversarial cases in full

Table 15 gives, for each case that Section 6.5 faces, the defence, what is enforced today in the working gate of Section 6.3, and the limit that remains. Every protection not enforced today is specified and not yet verified by an implementation test.

Table 15. The adversarial cases the gate must face: the defence, what is enforced today, and the limit that remains.
Case Defence Enforced today Limit that remains
Incorrect rules Rules written, reviewed and versioned; a rule’s author is not its deployer; each rule shown to deny a known positive case and allow a known negative one before deployment. Versioned rules in a schema-validated registry; invalid rules set aside and recorded. Separate review and the paired tests: specified. A wrong rule is enforced faithfully.
False evidence Provenance and signature checks; evidence accepted only from a procedure validated for that kind of input. Specified; the working gate reads only the content of the proposed call. A signature shows who signed, not that the content is true.
A manipulated evaluator The evaluator operated apart from the proposer, from another model family where a model is used, its agreement with human judgement measured and monitored (Zheng et al. 2023; Panickssery et al. 2024). Specified. Evaluators can share blind spots with the system they check.
A compromised policy The gate cannot edit its own rules; a rule change needs a separate authority and is versioned and recorded; a signed manifest of the gate’s files is checked at start-up. Models trained on gameable tasks have rewritten their own reward function (Denison et al. 2024), so the rules sit outside what the governed system can edit. The agent’s own tools pass through the gate, and rules are changed outside it; the signed manifest exists and is not yet running. An attacker with write access to the host can change the gate, its rules and its check.
Bypass Complete mediation: the adapter is the only route to the effect, and the proposer holds no credential (Saltzer and Schroeder 1975). Specified; the working gate mediates the tool calls of agent sessions only. A second route to the same resource defeats the boundary.
Time of check to time of use The broker checks again just before the effect, and the authorisation binds the resource’s version and a number used once, which the action consumes; the flaw is a check whose condition no longer holds when the action runs (Bishop and Dilger 1996). Specified. State that changes after the effect.
Rewritten records Each entry carries the hash of the one before; a separate verifier recomputes the chain; the latest hash is published or held by a witness, as audited tamper-evident logs and public certificate logs do (Schneier and Kelsey 1999; Crosby and Wallach 2009; Laurie et al. 2021). The chain and its verifier run; witnessing the latest hash: specified. Whoever can rewrite the whole log can rebuild the chain unless an independent copy of a later hash exists.
Gaming the rules Rules tested by a red team that assumes the proposer is trying to pass a harmful action, as control evaluations do (Greenblatt et al. 2023); no rule a proposer can satisfy by optimising a proxy where the property itself can be checked. Specified. Over all stochastic policies, a proxy and the true objective can be unhackable only if one of them is constant (Skalse et al. 2022).
Delay and flooding Time bounds on investigation; the precautionary default, which holds or applies an authorised fallback and never permits; the hold queue monitored by age, count and outcome; needless holds counted as a usefulness cost. Held calls are blocked, recorded with the rule that held them and saved across restarts; time bounds and queue monitoring: specified. A flood of holds can make a safe system useless (Section 7).
Override abuse Overrides only by a named authority, scoped and expiring, each recorded and reported. Every override is recorded; the issuer of the token is not verified. Whoever holds override power can let anything through.

G What this paper says, in plain English

Suppose that one day an AI system becomes more capable than the people who oversee it. The first rule of this paper is that people keep their hands on the controls, watching the system, limiting what it can do and able to switch it off, for as long as they physically can, and never let go by choice. A careful engineer still asks what happens if the controls are lost anyway. What would keep the system good then, and still useful?

The Eden Protocol answers in two parts. The first is a habit built into the system’s own working: at every step it checks its work before it keeps it. Does this step serve the purpose it was given? Who does it affect, including those with no voice? Would the reasoning hold if anyone used it anywhere? These are self-correction checks. The second part is a gate in front of every action. Before an action happens, a fixed set of written rules, and not the AI’s own opinion, decides whether it may go ahead, must wait while it is looked into, or is refused, and each decision goes into a record that cannot be quietly changed. A gate of rules is not perfect, and the paper lists the ways it could be fooled and what guards against each.

What should the checks care about? That is not for one author to decide. This paper tests whether checks built into each step work at all; what goes inside them should come from wide international agreement.

What has been found so far is small, and the paper says so. Telling AI models, in their instructions, to list everyone an answer affects before answering raised a scorer’s rating of how fully they considered those people, in all five model runs that could be analysed. But that was an instruction, not something built into the system; each run had a single scorer, which did not see which answers had the instruction but could still recognise its style; and the instruction asked for nearly what the score rewarded. In tiny networks that adjust themselves, building safety into what the network aims for helped it remember its old tasks. Neither result shows that the full idea works.

The first registered test of a prediction the Protocol rests on, Unit 83, was built so that it could fail, and it has now run. A record of a client’s money grew by one entry each round, with mistakes planted in the drafts. Two checkers were called every round. One, the corrector, worked inside the round: it saw the entries already kept, with the new entry marked, and could fix the new entry before it was kept. The other, the monitor, saw the whole record so far, with the new entry unmarked, and could only accept or reject it. If correcting inside the loop really matters more as the work grows longer, the corrector’s lead should grow round by round. Every entry was checked by computer against the right answer, so no one’s judgement was involved. The test ran on 27 and 28 October 2026, only after its plan had been published, and its own forecast, made before it ran, was split: under cautious assumptions a result against the idea was the likeliest single outcome, and under its central assumptions a result for it. Under its registered rules, P21, the prediction it tested, is supported under the registered test, by the programme’s own run, on the access axis, family-dependent, with its mechanism axis not evaluable and one call retried under a disclosed recovery amendment (results: DOI 10.17605/OSF.IO/98HKR). In plain words, correction placed inside each round held steady, while the monitor declined, and the corrector’s lead widened round by round; how much it widened depends on how an entry kept out of the record is scored. The result is family-dependent: the widening cleared the registered tolerance on one of the two engines and not on the other. The mechanism axis is not evaluable because a registered negative control failed, so the run does not explain why the lead widened: it may come from the corrector’s wider set of actions rather than from what the monitor can see. It is one owner’s run, on two engines he chose, at fixed weights, and it has not been replicated. The corrector acted inside each round at fixed weights: that is placement, not correction built into a system.

Finally, a safe AI that refuses ordinary work is a failure too. Every safety measure in this paper comes with a measure of usefulness beside it, so that safety is never bought by making the system useless.
